# Power Query Merge Creates Duplicate Rows? Fix Extra Rows

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-merge-duplicates-extra-rows
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Fix extra rows after a Power Query merge. Count matches before expanding, diagnose duplicate keys, and run downloadable M queries with a checked example.

## Related runnable tool

Inspect blank and repeated keys before a merge

Load the two source exports and map the proposed join key. Review blank or repeated keys in the unresolved report before assuming one match per record. The tool compares selected fields for unique keys; it does not simulate a Power Query join, count every join match or aggregate repeated sales amounts. Use the match-count query below for that diagnosis.

[Inspect source keys in the CSV comparison tool →](https://jhsoftlabs.com/workspace/compare-csv-files)

## Summary
Duplicate rows after a Power Query merge usually mean the chosen key matches more than one row in the other table. Before expanding, add Table.RowCount([Addresses]) as a Custom Column for the nested Addresses column. If the count exceeds 1, choose a genuinely unique reference key, define which record belongs to each sale, or keep only match counts when existence is all you need. A left outer join retains left records but does not guarantee one output row per record after expansion.

An Excel query with four sales can become six rows after you expand a merge. This is often a valid consequence of the selected keys, not a random refresh bug. The practical question is whether one output row should represent a sale, an address, or a sale-address pair.

## Worked example

```csv
sale_id,customer_id,amount
S1,C10,10
S2,C10,20
S3,C20,5
S4,C99,7

```

**Expected:** The four sales total 42. A left outer merge to three address records expands to six rows: both C10 sales appear twice, C20 once, and unmatched C99 once with empty right-side values. Summing the repeated amount column gives 72, which is not the original sales total.

### Explain the six rows before trying to delete them

This example uses Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows with two local Excel Tables named Sales and Addresses. customer_id is text in both. Addresses contains two different addresses for C10; neither row is an accidental duplicate. The requested merge key is customer_id, so both addresses satisfy the same customer match.

S1 has two matching address records and S2 has the same two matches. Those two sales therefore create four sale-address pairs. S3 creates one pair. A left outer merge also retains S4 even though C99 has no address. This arithmetic accounts for all six output rows. It also explains the inflated total: the extra copies of S1 and S2 add 30 to the original 42.

Quick diagnosis: if the row count rises only after Expand, count nested matches. If it rises before merging, inspect the source or append steps. If it doubles on every refresh even when the source is unchanged, check whether an output table or exported result is being read back into the input. The six-row example below isolates match multiplication; it does not diagnose every possible refresh loop.

**Figure: A duplicate key can describe valid detail**

Two C10 sales matched with two addresses produce four sale-address pairs, repeating the sale amounts.

Two C10 sales matched with two addresses produce four sale-address pairs, repeating the sale amounts.

Sales for C10:
S1 | 10
S2 | 20

Matching addresses:
A1 | Northport
A2 | Eastford

### Reproduce the merge and inspect its nested matches

Create the two source Tables from sales-input.csv and addresses-input.csv. Import each with Data > From Table/Range, set the identifier fields to Text, and use Close & Load To > Only Create Connection. Keep the source Tables separate from the final output Table so a refresh cannot ingest its own generated rows.

- Open the Sales query. Choose Home > Merge Queries > Merge Queries as New, then select Addresses as the second table.
- Select customer_id in both previews and choose Left Outer. Do not select fuzzy matching for these structured IDs.
- Before expanding the new Addresses column, add a Custom Column named address_matches with the expression Table.RowCount([Addresses]). The expected counts are 2, 2, 1 and 0 for S1 through S4.
- Expand address_id and city from Addresses. Keep the original sale_id so repeated sales are visible. Sort by sale_id and address_id for comparison with the expected CSV.
- Inspect the six output records. Do not treat a successful load as proof that the joined amount column can still be summed as one amount per sale.

### Choose the output grain that the report actually needs

If the report needs one row per sale with a single current address, the reference data must define which address is current. Obtain an explicit status, effective-date interval, or a sales shipping_address_id. Joining only on customer_id cannot supply a distinction that the data does not contain. A unique address key is useful only when it truly identifies the address recorded for that sale.

If the report needs all addresses, six rows are correct. Keep sale-level totals in the original Sales query or aggregate at sale_id before adding them to an address-level report. Do not sum a repeated sale amount across addresses unless you have a documented allocation rule. In this sample, no allocation rule is supplied, so inventing half an amount for each address would be an unsupported change.

### Use match counts when the task is only existence

Sometimes the real request is simply to label sales with an address on file. Stop before expansion and retain sale_id, customer_id, amount, and address_matches. Add a status of matched when the count is greater than zero and missing otherwise. This preserves four sales and the original amount total of 42. The separate match count still alerts you that C10 has multiple candidate addresses.

To audit the reference table independently, create a reference to Addresses, use Group By on customer_id with Count Rows, and filter counts greater than one. That audit identifies C10 without deleting A1 or A2. Grouping keys for an existence list is appropriate because only membership matters there; grouping full address records and arbitrarily keeping a city answers a different question.

**Figure: Existence does not need expansion**

Keeping nested-table counts preserves one record per sale while exposing multiple address matches.

Keeping nested-table counts preserves one record per sale while exposing multiple address matches.

Four source sales:
S1 amount 10
S2 amount 20
S3 amount 5
S4 amount 7

Four-row audit:
S1 matches 2
S2 matches 2
S3 matches 1
S4 matches 0

### Check composite keys and apparently identical IDs

An ID may be unique only within a company, warehouse, or year. If the declared key is company plus customer_id, select both columns in the same order on each side of the merge. First confirm the combined key is unique in the intended reference table. Adding arbitrary columns merely until the output becomes shorter can hide a modelling error.

Our sample uses exact text keys without case or whitespace normalization. For a production source, state whether C10 and c10 should be equivalent and whether surrounding spaces are accidental. Apply the agreed cleaning before both the duplicate audit and the join. Keep the original ID available for tracing, and do not convert zero-prefixed codes to numbers to make them match.

### Validate refreshes using more than a row count

Keep three independent controls: source sale count, source amount total, and a distribution of address_matches. For this input they are four, 42, and two sales with two matches, one with one match, and one with zero. The expanded result should contain six records, but that count is a diagnostic result rather than a target to force.

As a deliberate refresh test, add address A4 for C10 to the Addresses Table. The expected expanded count becomes eight: three rows for each C10 sale, one for C20, and one for C99. The four-row existence query should remain four rows and total 42. If either source count grows unexpectedly without such a change, check source ranges, appended files, and whether the query output was accidentally included in its input.

### Fix extra rows by choosing the right merge rule

Changing the join to Left Outer is not a uniqueness fix: it changes which unmatched rows survive. Similarly, replacing the merge with a lookup that returns one match does not establish that the first matching address is the intended one. Resolve the data rule first.

| What the report needs | Action before expansion | Check afterwards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One current address per sale | Use the actual address ID, a valid composite key, or an explicit current-record rule | Each sale has at most one right-side match |
| All sale/address pairs | Keep every valid match and retain sale_id | Six rows here; do not add repeated sale amounts |
| Whether a customer has an address | Keep the nested-table count without expanding | Four sales and amount total 42 |
| True duplicate copies in a reference export | Review which fields define an identical record before deduplicating | Reconcile removed records; do not drop distinct addresses |

### Run the match-count query before expanding

Load the two CSV samples into Excel Tables named Sales and Addresses. Keep their exact headers and set the identifier columns to Text before loading. Open Data > Get Data > From Other Sources > Blank Query, then Advanced Editor, and paste match-count-query.pq. This version reads the two named worksheet Tables, not other queries or a folder. If a query already has the same name as a source Table, the names here still refer to Tables returned by Excel.CurrentWorkbook.

The result is four rows with address_matches 2, 2, 1 and 0. When you need all sale/address pairs, use expanded-merge-query.pq as a separate query. It produces the six rows in expanded-expected.csv. Keep both outputs outside the source Tables; never name an output Table Sales or Addresses.

```powerquery
let
    SalesSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    AddressSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Addresses"]}[Content],
    Sales = Table.TransformColumnTypes(SalesSource, {{"sale_id", type text}, {"customer_id", type text}, {"amount", type number}}),
    Addresses = Table.TransformColumnTypes(AddressSource, {{"customer_id", type text}, {"address_id", type text}, {"city", type text}}),
    Merged = Table.NestedJoin(Sales, {"customer_id"}, Addresses, {"customer_id"}, "Addresses", JoinKind.LeftOuter),
    Counted = Table.AddColumn(Merged, "address_matches", each Table.RowCount([Addresses]), Int64.Type),
    Selected = Table.SelectColumns(Counted, {"sale_id", "customer_id", "amount", "address_matches"}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Selected, {{"sale_id", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted
```

### What we tested in the native Excel query engine

On October 5, 2026, the two downloadable queries were executed in Excel 16.0 build 5569.0 through the native M provider. The count-only output retained four sales totaling 42. The expanded output had six rows totaling 72 in its repeated amount column, including the unmatched sale S4. After adding a third C10 address and refreshing, expansion returned eight rows and repeated amounts totaled 102; the count-only query still returned four rows totaling 42.

This verifies the synthetic query behavior and refresh boundary, not every menu click or every Excel version. Compare the downloaded input/expected files and inspect the matches before using your own records.

[Identify hidden spaces before matching text keys](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/spreadsheet-trim-spaces)

[Find records with no match using a left anti join](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-left-anti-join-missing-rows)

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why did the row count change only after I clicked Expand?**

A: The merge stores matching right-side records in a nested table. Expansion exposes each match as a row, repeating the left fields for every matching record.

**Q: Should I remove duplicates from the final result?**

A: Only if your output contract defines those records as duplicates. A1 and A2 are different addresses in this example, so deleting one after the merge would discard valid detail.

**Q: How do I keep exactly one row per sale?**

A: Use a reference key that selects the intended single record, or retain a nested-table count when you only need match existence. An ambiguous one-to-many relationship needs a rule, not a cosmetic row deletion.

**Q: Does a Left Outer merge prevent duplicate rows?**

A: No. It retains unmatched left rows, but expanding several right-side matches still repeats the left fields. Count nested matches first and make the reference key or output rule explicit.

- [match-count-query.pq](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/power-query-merge-duplicates-extra-rows/match-count-query.pq)

```text
let
    SalesSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    AddressSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Addresses"]}[Content],
    Sales = Table.TransformColumnTypes(SalesSource, {{"sale_id", type text}, {"customer_id", type text}, {"amount", type number}}),
    Addresses = Table.TransformColumnTypes(AddressSource, {{"customer_id", type text}, {"address_id", type text}, {"city", type text}}),
    Merged = Table.NestedJoin(Sales, {"customer_id"}, Addresses, {"customer_id"}, "Addresses", JoinKind.LeftOuter),
    Counted = Table.AddColumn(Merged, "address_matches", each Table.RowCount([Addresses]), Int64.Type),
    Selected = Table.SelectColumns(Counted, {"sale_id", "customer_id", "amount", "address_matches"}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Selected, {{"sale_id", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted

```
- [expanded-merge-query.pq](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/power-query-merge-duplicates-extra-rows/expanded-merge-query.pq)

```text
let
    SalesSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}[Content],
    AddressSource = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Addresses"]}[Content],
    Sales = Table.TransformColumnTypes(SalesSource, {{"sale_id", type text}, {"customer_id", type text}, {"amount", type number}}),
    Addresses = Table.TransformColumnTypes(AddressSource, {{"customer_id", type text}, {"address_id", type text}, {"city", type text}}),
    Merged = Table.NestedJoin(Sales, {"customer_id"}, Addresses, {"customer_id"}, "Addresses", JoinKind.LeftOuter),
    Expanded = Table.ExpandTableColumn(Merged, "Addresses", {"address_id", "city"}, {"address_id", "city"}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Expanded, {{"sale_id", Order.Ascending}, {"address_id", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted

```

# Excel PivotTable Shows Count Instead of Sum: Fix the Source and the Value Field

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-pivot-table-count-instead-of-sum
**Category:** numbers-identifiers
**Description:** Change a PivotTable from Count to Sum, convert amount text safely, retain real blanks and zeros, and verify totals against a small source table.

## Summary
First repair the source amounts and verify their numeric types. Refresh the PivotTable, open Value Field Settings for the amount field, and choose Sum under Summarize Values By. Leave Show Values As set to No Calculation for an ordinary total. Check the result against both source totals and source record counts.

A PivotTable headed Count of Amount may be counting records when you expected a money total. Changing the summary setting is necessary, but the underlying field must also contain numeric values. A number format alone does not convert numeric-looking text into a number.

## Worked example

```csv
record_id,region,amount_text
R1,North,10.00
R2,North,20.00
R3,South,0.00
R4,South,5.00
R5,South,

```

**Expected:** The corrected report totals 35: North contributes 30 and South 5. There are five source records but only four recorded amounts. South includes a real zero and one truly missing amount. A separate Count of record_id gives North 2 and South 3; it is not a replacement for the amount total.

### Separate the summary choice from the source data type

This guide targets a normal worksheet-based PivotTable in Microsoft 365 Excel for Windows. It does not cover an OLAP cube or a custom Data Model measure, where field behavior and available calculations differ. The source is a five-row Table with record_id, region, and an amount_text field imported as text.

The two checks are independent. A clean numeric amount field can still have its summary set to Count from an earlier configuration. Conversely, a field set to Sum can omit text amounts and produce a misleadingly small result. Inspect both the field setting and the underlying source values instead of assuming that the visible heading tells you the data has been converted correctly.

**Figure: Two different questions need two fields**

Synthetic illustration: amount totals and record counts describe different properties of the same five source records.

Synthetic illustration: amount totals and record counts describe different properties of the same five source records.

Sum of amount:
North 30
South 5
Total 35

Count of record_id:
North 2
South 3
Total 5

### Create an intentionally inspectable source

Create an Excel Table named AmountSource from pivot-amounts-input.csv. Preserve the first two fields as Text. For a controlled reproduction of numeric-looking text, format the third column as Text before entering its four nonempty values, or import it explicitly as text. Leave the fifth amount cell genuinely empty, rather than typing a space or a formula returning an empty string.

Add a temporary helper column headed is_number and enter =ISNUMBER([@amount_text]). It should return FALSE for the four text values and for the missing value. Alignment and number formatting are not reliable substitutes for this check. Keep the raw column while converting a copy so you can verify that no amount, zero, or missing record was silently lost.

### Convert a copy without turning the missing amount into zero

Add a new Table column named amount_clean. For this fixture, the declared decimal separator is a dot and the grouping separator is a comma. Use the formula below to convert valid amount text while leaving missing input visibly empty. It intentionally lets invalid nonempty text raise an error instead of converting it to zero.

A formula result of an empty string is not the same as a genuinely empty source cell. Before using amount_clean for the final report, copy its results and Paste Special > Values into a new Table column named amount. Filter AmountSource for blank amount_text values and use Clear Contents on their corresponding amount cells; do not delete those source rows. Remove the filter and verify the missing R5 amount is truly blank.

```excel
=IF([@amount_text]="","",NUMBERVALUE([@amount_text],".",","))
```

### Build or repair the PivotTable calculation

Use the numeric amount column after the conversion check, not the original amount_text field. For an existing PivotTable, confirm its source includes that column and all five records, then refresh before changing its value setting. Updating cells outside the existing source range does not make them part of the report.

- Click inside AmountSource and select Insert > PivotTable, placing it on a new worksheet. For this walkthrough, leave Add this data to the Data Model unchecked.
- Place region in Rows and amount in Values. If the value field displays Count, open its menu and choose Value Field Settings.
- On Summarize Values By, select Sum. On Show Values As, use No Calculation for these ordinary totals. Apply a number format with two decimal places if desired.
- Add record_id as a second Values field and set that field to Count. It should count the five nonempty record IDs, including the record whose amount is missing.
- Compare North 30, South 5, and Grand Total 35 with pivot-summary-expected.csv. The record counts should be North 2, South 3, and total 5.

### Validate zero, missing values, and rejected text

R3 contains a recorded zero. It belongs in the four recorded amounts even though it contributes nothing to the sum. R5 has no recorded amount and belongs in a separate missing-value count. Replacing R5 with zero would leave the total at 35 while falsely increasing the number of recorded amounts to five.

On the final amount source column, COUNT should be 4 and SUM should be 35. On record_id, COUNTA should be 5 because all record identifiers are supplied. For a negative test, replace an input amount in a copy with pending. The conversion should fail visibly. A broad IFERROR(...,0) would hide that rejected value among legitimate zeros and make the report difficult to audit.

**Figure: An unchanged sum can hide fabricated completeness**

Illustrative completeness check: both versions total 35, but only the first preserves the missing R5 observation.

Illustrative completeness check: both versions total 35, but only the first preserves the missing R5 observation.

Correct source:
5 records
4 numeric amounts
1 truly missing amount

Missing replaced with zero:
5 records
5 numeric amounts
0 missing amounts

### Make recurring conversions refreshable

The helper-column path is useful for a small one-time repair because every cell can be inspected. For repeated imports, use a Power Query transformation that keeps source text, normalizes the agreed blanks to null, and applies an explicit number culture. Load the cleaned result to a new Table, then refresh that query before refreshing the PivotTable that depends on it.

Whichever route you use, keep the raw source and the rejected-value review together. A file with 1.234,50 needs a different numeric convention from this fixture. Do not strip all commas or punctuation as a universal fix. That could make a value parse while changing its magnitude. Use the source system specification and a known record to confirm the interpretation.

### Check what changed when the problem returns

If the PivotTable returns to Count after the field is removed and added again, inspect the refreshed source column for text, mixed values, and the current summary choice. Do not assume this means Excel changed a global preference. A new export may contain a textual placeholder or an empty-string formula that was absent from your first sample.

If Sum is selected but the number is still wrong, check source coverage, report filters, hidden field selections, and duplicate transactions. Refreshing does not decide which records should belong to a total. For a simple refresh test, add R6, North, 7.50 inside the source Table, run the same conversion, and refresh the report. Expected total becomes 42.50 with North 37.50, South 5, six records, and five recorded amounts.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does changing the cell format to Number solve this?**

A: No. It can change the display without changing text into numeric values. Check the source with ISNUMBER and use a conversion that matches the source punctuation.

**Q: Should I fill every blank amount with zero?**

A: Only if a blank actually means a recorded zero in your data contract. This example preserves one missing amount and one real zero, with different completeness counts.

**Q: Why is Sum selected but some amounts are still missing?**

A: Verify that the values are numeric, that the full source range is included, that the PivotTable was refreshed, and that filters or duplicate records are not changing the report.


# Excel FILTER #SPILL! Error: Find the Blocker Without Deleting Your Data

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-filter-spill-error
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Fix Excel FILTER spill errors with an exact three-row example. Check occupied cells, tables, merged cells, output size, and a separate no-match result.

## Summary
Enter =FILTER(A2:C6,B2:B6=K2,"No matching tickets") in F2, outside any Excel Table, with K2 set to North. The three matching records need F2:H4. Move any valuable content that blocks that rectangle, remove unwanted contents only after inspection, and keep merged cells outside the result area.

Your FILTER formula can be logically correct while Excel has nowhere to put its answer. The repair is to identify the intended output rectangle and inspect what occupies it. Replacing the formula repeatedly, wrapping it in IFERROR, or clearing an entire worksheet does not address that layout problem.

## Worked example

```csv
ticket,team,hours
T-01,North,2
T-02,South,5
T-03,North,3
T-04,West,4
T-05,North,1

```

**Expected:** With K2=North, F2:H4 contains T-01 / North / 2, T-03 / North / 3, and T-05 / North / 1. Total returned hours are 6. K2=East returns the single message No matching tickets.

### Reproduce a small, measurable result

Use Microsoft 365, Excel 2024, or Excel 2021 for the FILTER procedure. The English formulas here use commas as argument separators. Paste the sample into A1:C6 of a new worksheet, retaining its header row. Put North in K2 and manually copy the three header labels into F1:H1. F2 is the only cell where you enter the output formula; do not fill it across or down.

Before adding any deliberate obstruction, look at the expected file. There are three qualifying source rows and three returned columns, which means nine output cells. The row labels make the check independent of appearance: T-01, T-03, and T-05 must remain in that order, and the hours must stay attached to the right ticket. Do not include the source header in the filter range.

```excel
=FILTER(A2:C6,B2:B6=K2,"No matching tickets")
```

### Find the occupied cell inside the intended rectangle

In a copy of the exercise, type a note into G3 before entering the formula in F2. G3 is inside the required rectangle, so this is a useful controlled failure. Select F2 and inspect the spill boundary and the error menu. Where offered, Select Obstructing Cells takes you to the blocking entry. Move your note to a separate notes area rather than discarding it.

A cell that looks empty still deserves inspection in the formula bar. It may contain a space or a formula whose visible result is empty text. Test by moving the output to a clean area, not by deleting every apparently blank cell on a working sheet. Preserve a workbook copy first if the output area contains formulas maintained by another person. The output should appear when the obstruction is resolved.

**Figure: The answer needs a rectangle**

Illustrative cell map, not an Excel screenshot.

A note in G3 overlaps the middle row of the required F2 through H4 filter result.

Required output:
F2:H2: T-01
F3:H3: T-03
F4:H4: T-05

Example blocker:
G3 contains a note
Move the note elsewhere
Keep F2:H4 available

### Keep the output outside a Table and away from merges

It is reasonable to store the source in an Excel Table while placing the report beside it. The distinction is the formula location: a spilling result needs an ordinary worksheet area. If F2 belongs to a Table, move this report formula to a plain range. You do not need to dismantle a well-maintained source Table just to produce a filter report.

Merged headings cause a different collision. A wide merged title above the report can be harmless, but a merged range touching F2:H4 is part of the output space. Prefer moving the report to a clear sheet when unmerging would damage a designed form. Inspect the whole rectangle, including rows not visible on screen, before concluding that F2 itself is the only relevant cell.

### Plan for the result to grow when the criterion changes

The tiny sample has a maximum of five data rows, so a dedicated report area F2:H6 is enough for every possible single-team result. For a real export, reserve room for the largest permitted source dataset rather than only the current three matches. Do not place a grand total two rows under a live spill and assume it will stay out of the way next month.

Keep the source and condition ranges bounded and equally tall. In this exercise both begin on row 2 and end on row 6. If you extend one to row 500, extend the other deliberately and leave enough report space. A blank report worksheet is a practical choice when row counts vary widely. Place notes and criteria above the result or on a separate settings sheet.

**Figure: A changing result changes its footprint**

Reserve growth space; these future counts illustrate layout planning.

A report that grows from three to twenty rows would overlap a note just below the initial result.

Today:
North matches 3 rows
Uses F2:H4
A note in F5 appears safe

Larger future input:
North may match 20 rows
Needs F2:H21
The note would block it

### Separate a spill failure from an empty or broken condition

Change K2 to East. In this dataset that team does not exist, so the expected outcome is the readable no-match message supplied in the formula. This test answers a different question from clearing an obstruction: an empty set of qualifying tickets is a valid business result. Keep that message distinct from a generic error so the reader knows the filter ran.

If the error changes after the layout repair, inspect the inputs. The condition B2:B6 must describe the same five source records as A2:C6. An error stored in a condition cell needs its own correction; a wide IFERROR wrapper can hide it. A linked workbook adds another dependency, so copy the synthetic example into one workbook before diagnosing an external-link version.

### Verify the repaired report before relying on it

Confirm the three ticket identifiers, their order, and the total of 6 hours against the expected download. Change North to South: T-02 and 5 hours should be the only data row. Change it back to North to check the result can expand again. These criterion changes are more informative than a single screenshot of one successful state.

The downloads supply source and expected data, plus a setup note you can reproduce. They are synthetic, and the independent sample checks compare record-selection logic rather than running Excel itself. For a production workbook, also open it in the actual Excel version used by its recipient and test the output area after their usual filters, notes, and report refresh steps.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I fix FILTER #SPILL! by adding IFERROR?**

A: IFERROR does not create an empty spill range. Resolve the blocked or unsupported output location first, then use error handling only for an understood calculation error. Do not treat wrapping FILTER as a repair for a spill-placement problem.

**Q: Should I type the FILTER formula into every result cell?**

A: No. Enter it once at the top-left output cell. The resulting records occupy neighboring cells; editing those results requires changing the source or the originating formula.

**Q: Why does FILTER work until I select a different team?**

A: The new criterion may return more rows and collide with a note or another report. Keep room for the largest expected result and verify the new matched record count.

```text

T-01,North,2
T-02,South,5
T-03,North,3
T-04,West,4
T-05,North,1

```
- [filter-spill-expected.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/excel-filter-spill-error/filter-spill-expected.csv)

```text

```


# Count Checked Boxes in Google Sheets: Tasks, Categories and Completion Rate

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-countif-checkboxes
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Count checked and unchecked Google Sheets boxes without including empty template rows. Handle custom values and calculate a task-based completion rate.

## Summary
For default checkboxes, COUNTIF(range,TRUE) counts checked values. For a task report, use COUNTIFS with a nonblank task ID condition so empty template rows are excluded. Calculate completion against real tasks, and inspect the checkbox validation rule before using TRUE when custom values are configured.

A checklist may have checkboxes in hundreds of prepared rows but only a handful of real tasks. Counting every unchecked box makes the progress figure look much worse than the actual work. Custom checkbox values can also make a familiar TRUE formula return the wrong count.

## Worked example

```csv
task_id,category,done
T01,Setup,TRUE
T02,Setup,FALSE
T03,Review,TRUE
T04,Review,FALSE
T05,Review,TRUE
,,FALSE
```

**Expected:** There are five real tasks, three complete and two unchecked: 60% complete. The extra unchecked template row does not count as work. Setup is 1 of 2 complete and Review is 2 of 3 complete. The custom Done/Todo version must yield the same task counts.

### Create actual checkbox cells rather than trusting CSV text

Use Google Sheets in a desktop browser. Put task_id and category from the fixture into A1:B7 and done into C1. Select C2:C7 and use Insert > Checkbox. Check C2, C4 and C6; leave C3, C5 and C7 unchecked. C7 belongs to a template row with no task ID.

A CSV stores values, not checkbox validation rules. Importing the supplied TRUE and FALSE strings is therefore only a data reference, not a guarantee that your sheet contains interactive checkboxes. Inspect the formula bar or validation rule if the imported column behaves differently. The manual setup above makes the fixture's logical states explicit.

### Compare the simple count with the task count

Put the first formula below in E2 to count all checked states. It returns three. The second formula returns three unchecked values because it also includes C7. Both results accurately describe the selected checkbox cells, but only one unchecked count describes the real work.

For a progress report, make task_id the record boundary. A checkbox without a task ID is a prepared control, not a pending task. This distinction becomes important when a template contains hundreds of unchecked boxes. The rule should be written into the formula instead of depending on someone to stop selecting the range at exactly the right row.

```text
All checked values: =COUNTIF(C2:C7,TRUE)
All unchecked values: =COUNTIF(C2:C7,FALSE)
```

### Count completed and unchecked real tasks

Use the formulas below in E4:E6. They require a nonblank A cell, so the template row is excluded. Expected values are three completed tasks, two unchecked tasks and five total tasks. Keep each criteria range aligned to rows 2 through 7.

This example assumes every real task has exactly one default checkbox containing TRUE or FALSE. If a task's checkbox was deleted, the completed-plus-unchecked result may be smaller than the task total. Treat that mismatch as a data check. Do not quietly redefine every missing value as an unchecked task if a missing control signals an incomplete import.

```text
E4: =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<>",C2:C7,TRUE)
E5: =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<>",C2:C7,FALSE)
E6: =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"<>")
```

**Figure: A template row is not a task**

Illustrative task-based counting of synthetic checkboxes, excluding the blank-ID template row.

Source states; 5 task IDs; 3 checked + 2 unchecked; 1 extra unchecked template; Report counts; Completed: 3; Unchecked tasks: 2; Total tasks: 5

Source states:
5 task IDs
3 checked + 2 unchecked
1 extra unchecked template

Report counts:
Completed: 3
Unchecked tasks: 2
Total tasks: 5

### Calculate a rate with an explicit denominator

In E7 enter the formula below and format the result as a percentage. It divides the completed-task count by the number of task IDs, producing 60%. If there are no task IDs, it returns an empty display rather than reporting a meaningless zero divided by zero.

An empty rate and a 0% rate have different meanings: no tasks have been defined in the first case, while defined tasks remain incomplete in the second. Explain that distinction wherever the percentage is displayed. For this fixture, completed plus unchecked equals total; keep that simple reconciliation near the summary while you are building it.

```text
E7: =IF(E6=0,"",E4/E6)
Consistency check: =E4+E5=E6
```

### Add category totals without counting the template

Use G1:J3 for category, tasks, completed and completion. Put Setup in G2 and Review in G3. The formulas below go in H2:J2 and are filled down one row. Setup must be one completed task out of two; Review must be two out of three.

Keep task IDs nonblank and category spelling consistent. The category text in G2 is a criterion, not a formula fragment. A renamed category may create a zero-row report until the summary label changes. The download preserves the higher-precision ratios; the visible percentage may round Review to 66.67% depending on your chosen display format.

```text
H2: =COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$7,"<>",$B$2:$B$7,G2)
I2: =COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$7,"<>",$B$2:$B$7,G2,$C$2:$C$7,TRUE)
J2: =IF(H2=0,"",I2/H2)
```

### Use the configured values for custom checkboxes

Create the custom fixture on a separate tab. In Data > Data validation, inspect the Checkbox rule and its custom values. Set checked to Done and unchecked to Todo, then reproduce the same pattern of checked states. The COUNTIFS criteria must now use those text values rather than TRUE and FALSE.

The visual ticks are identical, but the cell values have changed. A weighted checkbox that stores a number is another model again: counting completed tasks and summing earned points are separate calculations. Keep one explicit convention per reporting range, or split the ranges by convention before combining totals.

```text
Completed custom tasks: =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<>",C2:C7,"Done")
Unchecked custom tasks: =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<>",C2:C7,"Todo")
```

**Figure: Same appearance, different stored values**

Illustrative value mapping; use the configured cell value as the counting criterion.

Default checkboxes; Checked -> TRUE; Unchecked -> FALSE; Custom checkboxes; Checked -> Done; Unchecked -> Todo

Default checkboxes:
Checked -> TRUE
Unchecked -> FALSE

Custom checkboxes:
Checked -> Done
Unchecked -> Todo

### Keep the checklist auditable as rows are added

Extend the task, category and checkbox ranges together. Before distributing the sheet, add one new real task and one empty template row on a copy. The real task should change the denominator; the template should not. Check that the consistency formula still returns TRUE and the category totals reconcile to the overall total.

The downloadable files validate states and arithmetic, not interactive checkbox behavior. Their independent checks do not create data validation or click controls in Google Sheets. A final native check should inspect default and custom rules, toggle one box, and confirm the summary updates. This article covers counting and progress; coloring a row from a checkbox is a separate presentation task.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why does my unchecked count include hundreds of rows?**

A: Prepared checkboxes can contain FALSE even where no task exists. Add a nonblank task ID criterion with COUNTIFS.

**Q: Why does TRUE stop counting after I customize the boxes?**

A: The checked value may now be text or a number. Inspect the validation rule and use that exact configured value.

**Q: Can I use COUNTA on the checkbox column for total tasks?**

A: It measures populated cells rather than real task records. Use the task-ID column for the denominator and validate the checkbox states separately.

- [checkbox-input.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/google-sheets-countif-checkboxes/checkbox-input.csv)

```text

T01,Setup,TRUE
T02,Setup,FALSE
T03,Review,TRUE

```
- [checkbox-summary-expected.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/google-sheets-countif-checkboxes/checkbox-summary-expected.csv)

```text

All,5,3,2,0.6
Setup,2,1,1,0.5
Review,3,2,1,0.6666666667
```
- [checkbox-custom-input.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/google-sheets-countif-checkboxes/checkbox-custom-input.csv)

```text

T01,Setup,Done
T02,Setup,Todo

,,Todo
```

```text
tasks,completed,unchecked
5,3,2
```

# Power Query Fill Down: Handle Nulls, Empty Text, and Group Boundaries

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-fill-down-null-values
**Category:** text-cleanup
**Description:** Fill repeated labels in Power Query while keeping leading blanks, zeros, and batch boundaries correct. Includes a grouped query and expected CSV.

## Summary
Sort by the original row sequence, convert agreed empty label text to null, and apply Fill Down to the label field only. If labels must not cross batches, fill inside each batch rather than across the entire table. A leading missing label has no predecessor and should remain unresolved, not borrow a label from another group.

Reports designed for people often show a department once and leave the following label cells blank. A machine-readable table needs that department beside every detail row. Fill Down can reconstruct those labels, but only when row order and group boundaries tell you which label is allowed to carry forward.

## Worked example

```csv
row_no,batch,label,value
1,B1,,5
2,B1,North,10
3,B1,,20
4,B1,South,30
5,B1,,40
6,B2,,50
7,B2,East,60
8,B2,,0

```

**Expected:** Eight rows remain and value totals 215. Labels in rows 3, 5, and 8 become North, South, and East respectively. Row 1 stays unlabeled because B1 has no earlier label; row 6 stays unlabeled because B2 starts a new batch. The zero in row 8 stays zero.

### State what a blank label is allowed to inherit

This walkthrough targets the Windows desktop Power Query Editor in Microsoft 365 Excel. The BatchRows Table contains two independent batches. Within one batch, a blank label means continue the preceding label. At the start of a batch, a blank label means the source has not supplied one yet. These two situations look similar in a worksheet but cannot be filled with the same global operation.

row_no records the source sequence. It is part of the sample contract and must be unique here. Sorting alphabetically by label before filling would destroy the relationship between headings and detail lines. If your source has no row number, add an index while the source is still in its meaningful order and preserve it through later steps. Do not invent an order after records have already been rearranged.

**Figure: Fill follows order inside a batch**

The first missing label has no earlier value; only later missing labels can inherit North.

The first missing label has no earlier value; only later missing labels can inherit North.

Batch B1:
Row 1: missing
Row 2: North
Row 3: missing

After grouped fill:
Row 1: still missing
Row 2: North
Row 3: North

### Distinguish null from text that only looks empty

Table.FillDown acts on null-valued cells. Empty text and spaces can look blank but are text values, so a label that appears empty may stop the fill or remain unfilled. For this example, null, empty text, and whitespace-only text are all missing labels. Nonempty labels are kept exactly as provided, including meaningful internal spaces.

The CSV fixture uses empty fields and cannot guarantee which blank representation every import route supplies. Inspect the query before filling. The provided M normalizes the label field using the explicit rule above. The separate blank-states.txt file describes additional checks with actual M null, an empty string, a string of spaces, and zero. Those tokens are descriptions, not instructions to type the word null into every empty source cell.

### Use the simple menu only for a single continuous group

If the entire source is one continuous report with no independent batch resets, the graphical workflow is short. Select only the categorical field that carries forward. Leave numeric amounts, row identifiers, and unrelated columns unselected. Filling every column would risk turning absent measurements into copies of the preceding measurement.

- Create BatchRows from batch-rows-input.csv as an Excel Table with headers, then use Data > From Table/Range.
- Set row_no to Whole Number and label to Text. Confirm the declared blank normalization has occurred before filling.
- For a single-group test, filter batch to B1, sort row_no ascending, select label, and choose Transform > Fill > Down.
- Verify row 1 remains missing, row 3 becomes North, and row 5 becomes South. The five B1 value cells must remain 5, 10, 20, 30, and 40.
- For the full two-batch source, use the grouped query below instead of removing the B1 filter and filling globally.

### Fill each batch independently with a complete query

This query groups by batch, sorts each group by row_no, fills only label, combines the resulting tables, and restores the overall row sequence. The final sort is explicit because a grouping operation should not be treated as an output-order guarantee. Load the result to a new worksheet and retain BatchRows as the source.

The batch identifier must describe the true reset boundary. If a report uses the same batch name for several unrelated blocks, add a unique block identifier first. Grouping all occurrences of an ambiguous name together could allow values to cross a boundary that the name does not capture. For the sample, B1 and B2 each occur in a single independent block, so batch is sufficient.

```powerquery
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="BatchRows"]}[Content],
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source, {{"row_no", Int64.Type}, {"batch", type text}, {"label", type text}, {"value", Int64.Type}}),
    Normalized = Table.TransformColumns(Typed, {{"label", each if _ = null or Text.Trim(_) = "" then null else _, type nullable text}}),
    Groups = Table.Group(Normalized, {"batch"}, {{"rows", each Table.FillDown(Table.Sort(_, {{"row_no", Order.Ascending}}), {"label"})}}),
    Combined = Table.Combine(Groups[rows]),
    Output = Table.Sort(Combined, {{"row_no", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Output
```

### Compare the grouped result with the unsafe global result

A global fill would place South in row 6 because row 5 carries South and row 6 follows it in the complete table. That is incorrect under the sample contract: row 6 belongs to B2, whose first supplied label is East in row 7. The grouped result leaves row 6 unresolved. This difference will not show up in the numeric grand total, which remains 215 in both cases.

The zero in row 8 is a measurement, not a missing label. It stays zero while its label becomes East. Similarly, a literal label such as None could be a meaningful category; do not convert every unusual word to null because it looks like a placeholder. Agree on source-specific placeholder values separately and test the count of affected records.

**Figure: A batch reset blocks inheritance**

Illustrative comparison: identical amount totals can hide an incorrect label carried across a batch boundary.

Illustrative comparison: identical amount totals can hide an incorrect label carried across a batch boundary.

Unsafe global fill:
B1 row 5: South
B2 row 6: becomes South

Grouped fill:
B1 row 5: South
B2 row 6: stays missing

### Validate and maintain the transformation

Compare all eight output records with batch-rows-expected.csv. Confirm two unresolved labels, three newly filled labels, unchanged row identifiers, and unchanged value total 215. These checks serve different purposes: the unresolved count catches fabricated labels, row identifiers catch lost detail, and the total catches accidental edits to value.

On refresh, add a new B2 row 9 with a missing label and value 4. It should inherit East, producing nine rows and value total 219. Then add a new batch B3 row 10 with a missing label and value 6: that label must remain missing. If it inherits East, inspect whether the fill moved outside the grouping step or whether B3 was incorrectly assigned the previous batch ID.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why does Fill Down do nothing to some blank-looking cells?**

A: They may contain empty text or spaces rather than null. Normalize only the placeholder forms that your data contract defines as missing, then fill the label column.

**Q: Can Fill Down cross a customer or batch boundary?**

A: A whole-table fill can. Group by the real boundary and sort inside each group before filling, as the sample query does for B1 and B2.

**Q: Should the first blank in each group become the next label?**

A: That would be a backward-fill rule, which this guide does not assume. A leading missing label remains unresolved unless the source explicitly defines it otherwise.

# Power Query Change Type Using Locale: Fix Dates and Decimal Commas

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-change-type-using-locale
**Category:** dates
**Description:** Fix Power Query date and number conversions with explicit source locales, a mixed-format example, expected output, and checks for silent day-month swaps.

## Summary
In Power Query Editor, return to the step where the original values are still text. Use Change Type > Using Locale on each affected column, selecting the source convention separately for dates and amounts. In this example dates use English (United Kingdom), while decimal-comma amounts use German (Germany). Keep the raw text until the converted output has been checked.

A query can refresh without errors and still contain the wrong dates. The value 03/04/2026 could mean April 3 or March 4, and a regional number convention can change the meaning of punctuation. Repairing this requires an import rule based on the source, rather than a different worksheet display format.

## Worked example

```csv
row_id,date_text,amount_text
R1,03/04/2026,"1.234,50"
R2,25/12/2026,"0,00"
R3,13/09/2026,"-25,75"
R4,,

```

**Expected:** Four rows remain. R1 is April 3, 2026 with amount 1234.50; R2 is December 25 with zero; R3 is September 13 with -25.75. R4 retains missing date and amount. The three recorded amounts total 1208.75. ISO dates in the expected CSV describe values, not a promise of Excel display formatting.

### Identify the convention before touching the query

This walkthrough targets Microsoft 365 Excel for Windows and the desktop Power Query Editor. The synthetic export intentionally combines day-first dates with German-style amount text. A real system might export both columns using one convention; it might also obtain them from different upstream services. Treat the convention as a property of each field, not evidence of where the person opening the workbook lives.

Ask which date R1 represents and verify the answer against a record with an unambiguous day, such as 25/12/2026. R2 tells us that a month-first parser cannot consistently explain this file. R1 alone cannot settle the issue. Do the same for amounts: the agreed value of 1.234,50 is one thousand two hundred thirty-four and fifty hundredths. Write these decisions beside the query before testing conversions.

**Figure: Two fields need two parsing rules**

Illustrative synthetic conversion: the date is day-first and the amount uses a decimal comma.

Illustrative synthetic conversion: the date is day-first and the amount uses a decimal comma.

Original text:
03/04/2026
1.234,50

Agreed values:
April 3, 2026
1234.50

### Import the raw file without losing the evidence

Save locale-input.csv and use Data > From Text/CSV, then Transform Data. Confirm comma is the file delimiter: quotation marks protect the comma inside amount_text. The field separator and the decimal separator perform different jobs. Changing the file delimiter to semicolon would not repair this comma-delimited sample.

Inspect Applied Steps before adding a correction. If an automatic Changed Type step has already interpreted date_text or amount_text, go to the preceding text step and remove or edit that early conversion. Merely changing an incorrectly parsed date back to text does not reconstruct its original characters. Preserve the CSV and duplicate the two raw columns if the final report needs both original and converted values.

### Apply a locale separately to the two columns

Use the original text columns for the following actions. For R4, inspect whether the blank fields arrived as null or as empty text; this example treats either as missing before conversion. It does not treat the literal strings NA or unknown as a missing-value agreement.

- Keep row_id as Text. Duplicate date_text and amount_text, naming the copies date and amount so the original strings remain available during review.
- For the date copy, normalize empty text to null if needed. Right-click its header, choose Change Type > Using Locale, select Date and English (United Kingdom), then confirm.
- For amount, apply the same missing-value rule. Choose Change Type > Using Locale with Decimal Number and German (Germany). Do not apply the date locale to this column just to keep the settings identical.
- Inspect R1, R2 and R3, including their day and month components. Remove the original text columns only in the final presentation query after comparison.
- Sort by row_id, then Home > Close & Load to a new worksheet. Retain the query and refresh it from the same unchanged input before trying another export.

### Run a complete query and keep the original text

For a repeatable alternative to the menu steps, download locale-conversion.pq and locale-input.csv. Create a Blank Query, open Advanced Editor, paste the query and set FilePath to the CSV on your computer. Only this local file is read. The result retains date_text and amount_text beside the converted date and amount, so you can inspect what changed before removing the originals.

The date helper accepts null as missing, parses with en-GB and compares the result formatted as dd/MM/yyyy with the original text. This round-trip check intentionally rejects 3/4/2026 under a two-digit day/month contract. It also keeps 31/02/2026 as an error. Change the contract explicitly if your exporter permits a different format; do not remove failing rows to make totals look correct.

Version finding: on our Excel 16.0 build 5569.0, the modern Date.FromText options record produced a Record-to-Text conversion error. Microsoft documents that record syntax for current engines. The download uses the older culture-text argument plus a separate exact-format check, which executed successfully on the tested build. This is a compatibility observation, not a claim that every Excel installation has the same engine.

```powerquery
let
    FilePath = "C:\CSVInput\locale-input.csv",
    Raw = Csv.Document(File.Contents(FilePath), [Delimiter=",", Encoding=65001, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.Csv]),
    Headers = Table.PromoteHeaders(Raw, [PromoteAllScalars=true]),
    EmptyToNull = Table.TransformColumns(Headers, {
        {"date_text", each if _ = "" then null else _, type nullable text},
        {"amount_text", each if _ = "" then null else _, type nullable text}
    }),
    ParseDate = (value as nullable text) as nullable date =>
        if value = null then null else
        let Parsed = Date.FromText(value, "en-GB")
        in if Date.ToText(Parsed, "dd/MM/yyyy", "en-GB") = value then Parsed
           else error "Expected an exact dd/MM/yyyy date: " & value,
    Dates = Table.AddColumn(EmptyToNull, "date", each ParseDate([date_text]), type nullable date),
    Amounts = Table.AddColumn(Dates, "amount", each Number.FromText([amount_text], "de-DE"), type nullable number),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Amounts, {{"row_id", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted
```

### Distinguish an error from a silent wrong answer

A conversion error is useful evidence that a value does not match the selected parser. A successful conversion proves less: both interpretations of 03/04/2026 are legitimate dates. Validate at least one ambiguous value against its intended meaning, rather than counting errors alone. The expected file makes R1 a deliberate check of this failure mode.

For a fixed export specification, Date.FromText can accept an explicit Format and Culture. For example, a column contract of dd/MM/yyyy deserves a format-specific conversion rather than best-effort interpretation. Number.FromText likewise accepts a culture. These functions are useful when the graphical transformation is too broad; they cannot discover the correct business meaning of an ambiguous string.

### Keep missing, zero, and rejected values separate

R2 amount zero is a recorded numeric value. R4 amount is missing, so the report has three recorded amounts across four source records. Filling R4 with zero would leave the total unchanged while changing that completeness count. Preserve this distinction if later calculations average amounts or measure missing data.

Add a test row R5 with date_text 31/02/2026 in a copy of the input. It is an invalid calendar date under the declared convention and should be investigated. A locale setting cannot make it valid. Keep an exception query or record the error; do not use Remove Errors merely to get a clean-looking report. The production extract should not quietly lose its rejected records.

**Figure: A total alone is insufficient**

Illustrative validation checks both row completeness and the meaning of an ambiguous date.

Illustrative validation checks both row completeness and the meaning of an ambiguous date.

Record checks:
4 source rows
3 numeric amounts
1 missing amount

Value checks:
Total 1208.75
R1 is April 3
R2 zero retained

### Make the next refresh repeatable

Keep a short import contract stating the source delimiter, encoding, date pattern, numeric culture, and missing-value rule. On the next export, compare those details before assuming the query remains valid. A new column label or a source system language change can require a different transformation even when the workbook itself has not changed.

If one column genuinely contains several conventions, split it using reliable provenance such as source_system and apply a parser to each subset. Do not guess by trying one culture and falling back to another: ambiguous values may succeed on the first attempt with the wrong interpretation. Combine the validated subsets afterwards, retaining an origin column so the rule remains auditable.

### What we ran in Excel, and how to reproduce it

On October 5, 2026, we executed the downloadable M query through the native Power Query provider in Excel 16.0 build 5569.0. All four rows remained: R1 became April 3, 2026 and 1234.50; R2 retained a numeric zero; R3 retained -25.75; R4 retained missing values. The three recorded amounts totaled 1208.75. These are engine execution results, separate from our earlier independent fixture calculations.

Three deliberate changes were tested separately: an impossible date, a nonnumeric amount and a date that violates the exact format. Each remained visible as an error on its source row. Use locale-native-checks.csv as a test checklist. In Power Query, keep an unchanged source copy, make one change, and use Keep Errors on the affected converted column to inspect the rejected row; restore the file before the next case.

The menu clicks, dialogs, Microsoft 365 online and Mac versions were not exercised by this native-provider test. Worksheet formatting can differ from the ISO dates in the expected CSV. Compare underlying dates and numbers, not just their appearance.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Will changing Excel cell formatting fix this?**

A: No. Formatting changes how an existing value appears. This workflow repairs the interpretation while the original source is still text; an already incorrect date needs to be rebuilt from that source.

**Q: Why does Using Locale still produce errors?**

A: Check the earliest type step, the raw characters, impossible dates, and whether the input mixes conventions. Keep the rejected records for review instead of replacing all errors with zero or null.

**Q: Can a single query use different locales?**

A: Yes. Apply separate conversion steps to fields with different declared conventions. The sample intentionally uses day-first date text and German-style numeric punctuation.

# PivotTable Missing New Rows After Refresh? Check Its Source Range

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-pivot-table-missing-new-rows
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Include new rows in an Excel PivotTable by checking its source range, switching to an Excel Table, refreshing, and checking filters against sample totals.

## Summary
Check the PivotTable’s source before refreshing again. Expand a fixed range to include the new rows, or point the PivotTable to an Excel Table that includes them. Then refresh and compare both record counts and totals; refresh alone does not expand a fixed source range.

You append this month’s records, click Refresh, and the PivotTable still shows last month’s total. The missing rows may sit outside its source, even though they look like part of the same worksheet list.

## Worked example

```csv
order_id,region,amount
O101,East,40
O102,West,60
O103,East,20
O104,West,30
O105,East,50
O106,West,10

```

**Expected:** The initial four orders total 150: East 60 and West 90. After including O105 and O106, six orders total 210: East 110 and West 100. These totals assume all PivotTable filters are cleared and amount uses Sum.

### Reproduce the missing-row problem

Use a fresh desktop Excel workbook for this example. Enter the initial file’s header and four records in A1:C5. Keep order_id and region as text and amount as numeric values. Name the worksheet OrdersData. Select A1:C5, choose Insert > PivotTable, and place the report on a new worksheet.

Put region in Rows and amount in Values. Confirm the value field says Sum of amount rather than Count of amount. With no filters, East is 60 and West is 90. Now append the expanded file’s two extra records at A6:C7. Do not paste its header a second time. The worksheet total has changed, but a source still ending at row 5 cannot read those additions. A desktop Excel 16.0 build 5569 reproduction on September 19, 2026 kept the total at 150 after refreshing that fixed source, then returned 210 after the source was expanded through row 7.

**Figure: A refresh can read the wrong boundary**

Synthetic source-boundary example. Both ranges include one header row.

The old source includes four orders and excludes the two appended orders worth 60.

Fixed source:
OrdersData!A1:C5
4 orders; total 150

Actual data:
OrdersData!A1:C7
6 orders; total 210

### Repair the fixed range once

Click inside the existing PivotTable. On PivotTable Analyze, choose Change Data Source. Some versions label the contextual tab Analyze. Inspect Table/Range instead of assuming the highlighted source reaches the last record.

- For this example, replace OrdersData!$A$1:$C$5 with OrdersData!$A$1:$C$7. Include the header once and every data row, without unrelated notes or a worksheet grand total.
- Confirm the change, then right-click inside the PivotTable and choose Refresh.
- Clear PivotTable field filters, slicers, and timelines while checking the example. A filter can hide a newly added record even when the source includes it.
- Verify East 110, West 100, and Grand Total 210. If the total is 6, the value field is probably counting records instead of summing numeric amounts.

### Use an Excel Table for future additions

A Table gives the source a name and a boundary that can grow. Converting the worksheet list is only half the repair: explicitly check that the existing PivotTable now refers to the Table name rather than its old address.

- On OrdersData, select A1:C7 and choose Insert > Table. Confirm My table has headers. Under Table Design, set the Table Name to Orders.
- Return to the PivotTable and open Change Data Source. Set Table/Range to Orders, confirm, and refresh.
- Append subsequent records immediately below the last Table row, or insert Table rows. Check that they are inside the Table; matching colors alone are not proof.
- If a paste falls outside the Table, click within it and use Table Design > Resize Table to include the intended rectangle. Then refresh the PivotTable.

### Separate source coverage from refresh timing

A Table’s growth and a PivotTable’s refresh are separate events. Keep an explicit Refresh step in the reporting checklist, especially when another person opens the workbook in a different Excel version.

As checked on September 19, 2026, Microsoft’s support page labels PivotTable Auto Refresh as available to Microsoft 365 Insider participants. Do not assume every installation updates immediately after an edit. The older refresh-on-open option also differs from refreshing whenever source cells change. None of these settings fixes a source that excludes the new rows.

| Situation | Check | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed address ends before new rows | Table/Range ending row | Expand the range or use a Table |
| Table source; new rows outside it | Actual Table boundary | Resize the Table, then refresh |
| Correct source; total still old | Refresh and report filters | Refresh, clear filters, compare totals |
| Power Query or Data Model source | Connection and query output | Refresh upstream data; inspect that source |
| Counts instead of monetary totals | Value field aggregation and types | Use numeric amount with Sum |

### Reconcile an independent count and total

Check the input separately from the report. For the six-row Orders Table, the formulas below should return 6, 6, and 210. If COUNT is smaller than ROWS, at least one amount is blank or nonnumeric; identify it before trusting a sum.

Also inspect both appended IDs. A grand total can accidentally remain correct if one record is duplicated and another is omitted. The regional subtotals give a second check, and the source IDs give a third. Keep these checks beside a recurring report so the next refresh can be reviewed quickly.

```excel
=ROWS(Orders[order_id])
=COUNT(Orders[amount])
=SUM(Orders[amount])
```

**Figure: Expected report after including all rows**

Synthetic sums for the two downloadable order files.

Adding an East order of 50 and a West order of 10 changes the total from 150 to 210.

Before additions:
East: 60
West: 90
Grand total: 150

After additions:
East: 110
West: 100
Grand total: 210

### Recognize when the source is an external query

This walkthrough targets a PivotTable built from a worksheet range or Table in the same workbook. If Change Data Source shows a connection or Data Model, inspect the query and loaded result instead. Changing an unrelated worksheet range will not repair that connection.

For query-backed reports, wait for the upstream refresh to complete, confirm that its output contains the new IDs, and then refresh the report. Preserve the existing workbook before rebuilding anything; a replacement PivotTable can require recreating its fields, filters, and dependent report references.

[Combine recurring CSV exports before building a report](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/combine-csv-files-excel)

### Tested source-range boundary

In desktop Excel 16.0 build 5569 on September 19, 2026, refreshing the PivotTable left the total at 150 while two appended records were outside the fixed A1:C5 source. After expanding the source through row 7, the PivotTable total became 210.

This is one synthetic workbook and one Excel build, not a test of every interface or data model. For your workbook, first inspect the actual PivotTable source and record counts; then refresh after changing the source to include the new rows.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why does Refresh All still miss new rows?**

A: A fixed source range can exclude them, or the report can filter them out. Inspect the source’s final row and clear report filters before concluding that refresh failed. For an external query, first confirm its refreshed output contains the new records.

**Q: Does formatting the source as a Table fix my existing PivotTable automatically?**

A: Do not rely on that alone. Open Change Data Source and confirm the PivotTable uses the Table name. Then check the Table includes the appended records and refresh the report.

**Q: Should I use an entire column as the PivotTable source?**

A: A defined Table is usually easier to audit. An entire-column source can include unrelated entries and many blanks. For this example, Orders contains only the three intended columns, one header, and six records.
