# Remove Completely Blank Rows in Excel Without Losing Partial Records

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-remove-blank-rows-safely
**Category:** text-cleanup
**Description:** Use a row-wide COUNTA check to remove completely blank Excel rows while keeping partial records, zero amounts, and the original data intact.

## Summary
Test all columns belonging to each record with =COUNTA(A2:D2)>0. Keep TRUE rows and copy their visible cells to a clean worksheet. This produces a blank-row-free data snapshot while preserving records that contain a missing customer, a zero amount, or an empty note.

A list can contain empty separator rows and legitimate records with missing fields. Selecting every blank cell does not distinguish those cases, so deleting the selected cells or their rows can damage the list.

## Worked example

```csv
order_id,customer,amount,note
O101,Ada,25,paid
O102,,40,pending
,,,
O103,Bo,0,waived
,,,
O104,Cy,15,

```

**Expected:** Keep O101, O102, O103, and O104 in that order. Remove only the two rows whose four source cells are empty. The cleaned result has four records and an amount total of 80; O102 still has no customer and O103 still has numeric zero.

### Decide what counts as an empty record

For this example, one record occupies columns A:D. A row is removable only when all four cells are empty. The empty customer in O102 is missing information within an otherwise valid order. The zero amount in O103 is a recorded value, not a blank.

Choose the full record width before writing the formula. If your real data extends through column K, checking A:D is insufficient. A note, status, or identifier in E:K means that row contains data. Exclude unrelated side tables from the record definition, and keep the cleanup output on a separate worksheet.

**Figure: A blank field is not a blank row**

Synthetic row classification across the complete four-column record.

The order with a missing customer is kept because its ID, amount, and note still contain values.

Partial order:
O102 | [blank] | 40 | pending
Keep this record

Empty record:
[blank] in all four fields
Remove this separator row

### Add a conservative row-wide helper

Enter the sample header and six data rows in A1:D7 of a fresh worksheet. The two comma-only CSV records correspond to empty cells across A4:D4 and A6:D6. If you paste from a text viewer, make sure the data actually occupies four columns before continuing.

- Save an untouched copy of the workbook. For a data-export workflow, work on a duplicate worksheet containing the same records.
- Enter keep_row in E1 and =COUNTA(A2:D2)>0 in E2. Fill E2 down through E7 only; do not extend across unused worksheet rows.
- Check the flags in source order: TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE. Investigate any difference before filtering.
- Select A1:E7, choose Data > Filter, and use the keep_row dropdown to display TRUE only. The four orders should remain visible.

```excel
=COUNTA(A2:D2)>0
```

### Make a compact copy of the kept records

The following copy procedure is for Windows desktop Excel. It avoids deleting worksheet rows that might also contain another table. For this plain export, the desired deliverable is a values-only snapshot; the original workbook remains the source of record.

- With keep_row filtered to TRUE, select A1:D7, including the header but excluding the helper column.
- Choose Home > Find & Select > Go To Special > Visible cells only, then OK. This explicitly excludes hidden or filtered rows from the selection.
- Copy the selection. On a new, unfiltered worksheet, choose A1 and use Paste Special > Values. Confirm that the records occupy A2:D5 without separator rows.
- Reapply number and date formats if needed, then verify the output against the expected file. Save the cleaned snapshot under a new name.

### Treat formulas and invisible characters deliberately

COUNTA counts a formula that returns an empty string. It also counts spaces, errors, and zero. This deliberately favors keeping ambiguous rows so you can review them instead of discarding them.

A values-only copy does not preserve formulas: it records their current results. If the working workbook must retain calculations, keep it unchanged and use the helper filter as a view, or produce a separate reporting snapshot. Do not replace a calculation workbook with the snapshot.

| Source content across a row | Helper result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All record cells genuinely empty | FALSE | Removable under this rule |
| ID present; customer missing | TRUE | Incomplete record to keep |
| A numeric zero | TRUE | Recorded value to keep |
| Formula returning an empty string | TRUE | Formula exists; review separately |
| A space or nonbreaking space | TRUE | Text exists; review before clearing |
| An error value such as #N/A | TRUE | Broken value; do not silently discard |

### Verify records, positions, and totals

The cleaned output contains one header and four orders. Compare the exact order IDs and their sequence, then confirm the sum of amounts is 80. Check O102’s empty customer and O104’s empty note remain in their original columns. Preserving row alignment matters as much as removing visual gaps.

For this sample, enter =COUNTA(A2:A5) and =SUM(C2:C5) beside the clean output to obtain 4 and 80. The first formula works here because every valid order has an ID; do not reuse it as a general proof when IDs can be missing.

```csv
order_id,customer,amount,note
O101,Ada,25,paid
O102,,40,pending
O103,Bo,0,waived
O104,Cy,15,
```

**Figure: Remove two empty records, preserve four orders**

Synthetic before-and-after checks; the original source is retained.

Removing the two fully empty rows keeps four orders and leaves the amount total unchanged at 80.

Input:
6 data rows
2 completely empty
Amount total: 80

Clean snapshot:
4 data rows
Same four order IDs
Amount total: 80

### Avoid the shortcuts that mix records

Go To Special > Blanks selects individual empty cells, not only completely empty records. Deleting those cells with Shift cells up can move a customer name independently from its order ID. Deleting entire rows based only on blanks in customer would also remove O102.

Filtering one column for blanks is safe only if a documented business rule says that column must exist for every record you intend to retain. A cleanup guide cannot assume that rule. Use the full-width helper when the task is specifically to remove completely empty rows.

If rows appear blank because they are hidden, filtered, or formatted with invisible text, inspect those conditions before cleanup. The helper removes neither formatting nor hidden characters. Review uncertain cases in the source and rerun the same checks after any deliberate edits.

[Inspect hidden spaces before treating text as empty](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/spreadsheet-trim-spaces)

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why did Go To Special > Blanks delete some real orders?**

A: It selects blank cells within partially filled records. Deleting their entire rows removes the other fields too, while shifting individual cells can break alignment. Restore the original and classify each complete record with the helper.

**Q: Why does COUNTA keep a row that looks blank?**

A: A formula returning empty text, a space, an error, or another stored value counts as content. Inspect the formula bar and all record columns before deciding that the row should be removed.

**Q: Does this method preserve formulas and formatting?**

A: The source copy does. The compact output procedure intentionally pastes values for a data snapshot, so it does not retain formulas or all formatting. Keep the original calculation workbook and reapply the output formats you need.

- [blank-row-input.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/excel-remove-blank-rows-safely/blank-row-input.csv)

```text
order_id,customer,amount,note
O101,Ada,25,paid
O102,,40,pending
,,,
O103,Bo,0,waived
,,,
O104,Cy,15,

```
- [blank-row-expected.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/excel-remove-blank-rows-safely/blank-row-expected.csv)

```text

O102,,40,pending
O103,Bo,0,waived
O104,Cy,15,

```

# Excel TEXTSPLIT with Multiple Delimiters: Keep Empty Fields in the Right Column

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-textsplit-multiple-delimiters
**Category:** text-cleanup
**Description:** Split Excel text on commas, semicolons, and pipes with TEXTSPLIT. Preserve empty fields, handle row delimiters, and avoid mistaking simple splitting for CSV parsing.

## Summary
In supported Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024, enter =TEXTSPLIT(A2,{",",";","|"},,FALSE) in C2. Copy the formula only down to C3 for the second source string. FALSE preserves a field between consecutive delimiters; TRUE is appropriate only when the output is an unstructured list where those empty positions do not matter.

Mixed separators are easy to fix until one record contains a missing field. If you discard the empty segment, the remaining values shift into the wrong columns while still looking tidy. This example splits a four-field record on three delimiters and keeps a missing region in its original position.

## Worked example

```csv
case,raw_text
mixed,"R-07,North;High|Open"
missing_field,"R-08,,Low|Closed"

```

**Expected:** R-07 splits into R-07 / North / High / Open. R-08,,Low|Closed splits into R-08 / empty region / Low / Closed when empty fields are preserved. Ignoring empty fields shifts Low into the second position.

### Check availability and prepare two source strings

This guide targets current Microsoft 365 and Excel 2024 editions that support TEXTSPLIT. Do not assume the function exists in Excel 2021 or earlier simply because those editions support other dynamic arrays. If Excel shows an unknown function name, verify the installed version before investigating separators or changing the data.

For the worksheet procedure, put R-07,North;High|Open in A2 and R-08,,Low|Closed in A3. Put record, region, priority, and status in C1:F1. The downloadable CSV has a case label and a quoted raw_text field for documentation, so copying its entire table into A1 would create a different layout. Copy the raw_text strings alone into the stated cells or use the setup text file.

### Split on any of three alternative delimiters

Enter the formula once in C2 and copy C2 down to C3. Each formula reads one source cell and returns horizontally across the row. The array constant identifies comma, semicolon, and pipe as alternative field boundaries; these are not three sequential cleanup passes. Leave the destination cells C2:F3 clear before entering the formulas.

For row 2, the output should be R-07 in C2, North in D2, High in E2, and Open in F2. Check both the labels and the positions. This tiny fixture is intended to make a shifted field obvious, which is harder when a production record has dozens of similar-looking numeric fields.

```excel
=TEXTSPLIT(A2,{",",";","|"},,FALSE)
```

**Figure: Three delimiters, one record layout**

An explanatory map of the synthetic record, not an Excel screenshot.

The comma, semicolon, and pipe boundaries produce four fields in the requested column order.

Source string:
R-07,North;High|Open
Comma separates record
Semicolon and pipe also split

C2:F2 result:
R-07 | North
High | Open
Four fields, original order

### Preserve the missing region instead of shifting the record

Row 3 contains two consecutive commas after R-08. The segment between those commas represents a missing region, not an accidental extra punctuation mark under this record contract. With FALSE, D3 remains an empty field, Low stays in E3 under priority, and Closed stays in F3 under status.

Try the TRUE variation in a separate result area H3, with four empty cells available. That result has three fields: R-08, Low, and Closed. It is a reasonable compact list, but it is wrong if you label the second field region. Keep the two outputs separate while comparing them rather than overwriting the correct result with an experimental formula.

```excel
=TEXTSPLIT(A3,{",",";","|"},,TRUE)
```

**Figure: Empty fields carry a position**

The second result has three fields and cannot use the same four-column schema unchanged.

Ignoring the missing region shifts priority and status one column to the left.

Preserve empty fields:
record: R-08
region: empty
priority: Low; status: Closed

Discard empty fields:
position 1: R-08
position 2: Low
position 3: Closed

### Separate row delimiters from column delimiters

A different input can contain multiple records inside one cell. For a separate exercise, put R-11,North|R-12,South in A6 and enter the formula below in C6. Here comma separates fields across columns, while pipe separates records down rows. C6:D7 should contain two records, each with two fields.

Do not add pipe to the column delimiter list at the same time when it is meant to mark a new record. A separator has a structural role defined by the export format. Decide whether it means another field, another record, or literal content before choosing a formula. Otherwise a superficially successful split can flatten multiple records into one long row.

```excel
=TEXTSPLIT(A6,",","|",FALSE,0,"[missing]")
```

### Distinguish missing padding from an explicitly empty field

Change A6 to R-11,North|R-12 for one further test. The second record now has fewer fields than the first. With the same formula, C7 contains R-12 and D7 contains the chosen marker [missing]. That marker makes an uneven record visible to the reviewer instead of silently pretending the export was complete.

A missing trailing field in an uneven row and an explicitly empty segment between two separators are related but different cases. Keep a validation column or a review note for each rejected record when adapting this to a recurring import. The split formula tells you where fields are; it does not prove that every required field was supplied or that each value has the intended meaning.

### Use a CSV importer for quoted CSV records

The mixed-delimiter examples assume separators never occur as literal characters inside a field. A genuine CSV record can contain a quoted value such as "North, East", where the comma is part of the value. Splitting every comma without handling quoting would divide that one value incorrectly. Use an import path that understands CSV quoting for that case.

Also review what should happen to surrounding spaces and numeric-looking identifiers. This guide preserves the text tokens as written and does not coerce them into dates or numbers. Test identifiers with leading zeros separately before adding a conversion step. Keep the original string until the mapped output passes a field-count and value check.

The accompanying expected files cover both empty-field policies and the two-dimensional example. Independent checks reproduce these synthetic delimiter rules in Python; they do not run Excel or promise general CSV compatibility. Before using the formulas at scale, test the actual delimiter characters and argument separators in your installed Excel locale.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How do I specify more than one delimiter in TEXTSPLIT?**

A: Use an array constant such as {",",";","|"} for alternative column delimiters. The sample uses English formula separators; Excel locale settings may require a different separator syntax.

**Q: Should I set ignore_empty to TRUE?**

A: Only when empty segments have no positional meaning. For fixed fields such as record, region, priority, and status, preserving a missing region prevents later fields from shifting.

**Q: Can TEXTSPLIT replace a CSV parser?**

A: Not for general quoted CSV. These examples assume delimiters are actual boundaries and cannot appear literally inside quoted fields. Use a CSV-aware import for quoted commas, quotes, or embedded record breaks.

```text

```


```text

R-11,North
R-12,South

```

```text
C2: =TEXTSPLIT(A2,{",",";","|"},,FALSE)

C6: =TEXTSPLIT(A6,",","|",FALSE,0,"[missing]")

```

# Excel WORKDAY with Holidays: Add Business Days Without an Off-by-One Error

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-workday-holidays
**Category:** dates
**Description:** Calculate Excel business-day deadlines with WORKDAY and WORKDAY.INTL. Check start-day counting, real holiday dates, custom weekends, and sample results.

## Summary
Use =WORKDAY(A2,B2,$H$2:$H$3) to move B2 working days after A2, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and your holiday list. The positive count begins after the starting date. Use WORKDAY.INTL for a different weekend and an explicit inclusive formula when the first eligible date must count as day one.

A deadline that is one day early or late often comes from a counting rule rather than a broken formula. Establish whether the starting date counts as day one, which days are weekends, and which exact dates your calendar excludes.

## Worked example

```csv
case,start_date,workdays,weekend,holidays
standard,2026-09-04,3,Saturday/Sunday,2026-09-07 and 2026-09-10

```

**Expected:** For Friday September 4, 2026 plus 3 working days, with September 7 and 10 excluded, the result is Friday September 11. Counting September 4 as day one instead gives Wednesday September 9. The closure dates are synthetic examples, not a national holiday calendar.

### Build a calendar with real Excel dates

Create the small setup below in a fresh worksheet. Enter the DATE formulas rather than pasting ambiguous strings such as 09/04/2026. Format A2, C2, and H2:H3 as yyyy-mm-dd so their displayed meaning is clear.

The two closure dates are invented for this exercise. Excel does not fetch public holidays automatically. For a real report, obtain the relevant workplace calendar, include observed closure dates, and keep its owner and year documented. An empty or outdated list changes the deadline.

```text
A1: start_date        B1: workdays       C1: deadline
A2: =DATE(2026,9,4)    B2: 3
H1: excluded_dates
H2: =DATE(2026,9,7)
H3: =DATE(2026,9,10)
C2: =WORKDAY(A2,B2,$H$2:$H$3)
```

### Trace the three counted working days

September 4 is the starting point. With a positive offset, it is not day one. September 5 and 6 are weekend days, September 7 is excluded, and September 8 is the first counted day. September 9 is second; the excluded September 10 is skipped, so September 11 is third.

This trace is more useful than repeatedly changing the formula until a date looks right. If your result differs, first inspect the source dates and count convention, then inspect the holiday range. A date stored as text may look identical to a numeric date in a formatted cell.

**Figure: Three workdays after September 4**

Synthetic calendar with Saturday/Sunday weekends and two explicit closures.

The third eligible working date after September 4 is September 11 because two closures and the weekend are excluded.

Skip these dates:
Sep 5–6: weekend
Sep 7: closure
Sep 10: closure

Count these dates:
Sep 8: day 1
Sep 9: day 2
Sep 11: day 3

### Choose an exclusive or inclusive start rule

For a promise phrased as “three business days after receipt,” the standard formula matches an exclusive start. For a three-day task whose first eligible date is day one, use the inclusive alternative below. It begins from the calendar day before the requested start, so the next eligible day can be counted.

The inclusive formula assumes B2 is a positive integer. It also handles a Saturday or holiday start by counting the first eligible date on or after that start. Simply subtracting one from B2 is insufficient when A2 itself is not a working day.

```excel
=WORKDAY(A2-1,B2,$H$2:$H$3)
```

| Question for the sample | Formula rule | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 workdays after September 4 | WORKDAY(A2,3,holidays) | 2026-09-11 |
| 3-day task starting on September 4 | WORKDAY(A2-1,3,holidays) | 2026-09-09 |
| 1 workday after Saturday September 5 | WORKDAY(DATE(2026,9,5),1,holidays) | 2026-09-08 |
| 3 workdays before September 11 | WORKDAY(DATE(2026,9,11),-3,holidays) | 2026-09-04 |

### Use WORKDAY.INTL for a custom weekend

WORKDAY assumes Saturday and Sunday are nonworking days. For a Friday/Saturday weekend, use WORKDAY.INTL and the quoted string "0000110". Its seven positions run from Monday through Sunday: 1 excludes that day and 0 allows it.

With a Thursday September 3 start, three subsequent workdays under that pattern, and the same two closures, the result is September 9. Friday and Saturday are skipped, Sunday September 6 counts as day one, Monday is a closure, Tuesday is day two, and Wednesday is day three. Keep the weekend pattern next to the report rather than leaving readers to infer it.

```excel
=WORKDAY.INTL(DATE(2026,9,3),3,"0000110",$H$2:$H$3)
```

**Figure: A different weekend changes the sequence**

Both examples happen to end on September 9, but they count different first days.

Changing the weekend allows Sunday September 6 instead of Friday September 4; the closure on September 7 remains excluded.

Saturday/Sunday off:
Start: Thu Sep 3
Fri Sep 4 counts
Then Tue Sep 8, Wed Sep 9

Friday/Saturday off:
Start: Thu Sep 3
Sun Sep 6 counts
Then Tue Sep 8, Wed Sep 9

### Check holidays, copying, and result formatting

Use =ISNUMBER(A2) and =ISNUMBER(H2) as quick checks that these cells contain numeric dates, then inspect their displayed dates. A numeric result alone does not prove the correct day was entered. Keep the absolute holiday reference when filling C2 downward; otherwise the excluded range can slide to different cells.

WORKDAY returns an Excel date serial. If the result appears as a large integer, apply a date format instead of subtracting an arbitrary offset. Keep the result numeric when another formula or sort will use it; TEXT creates a display string.

Use whole-day offsets. Fractional offsets are truncated, so WORKDAY is not a calculator for shifts, half-days, or elapsed working hours. WORKDAY.INTL with an offset of zero returns the specified start date; it is not a general instruction to advance a weekend date to Monday.

[Understand numeric date serials and display formats](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/excel-date-serial-numbers)

### Make the scheduling rule reviewable

Store the start, duration, holiday list, weekend rule, and computed deadline separately. This lets another reader explain the result without reverse-engineering a long formula. Before using a new year’s calendar, test a normal weekday, a weekend start, a closure start, and a date crossing year-end.

The downloadable setup reproduces this synthetic example. It does not include actual regional holidays or local working-time rules. Choose those inputs for your own workflow and verify one short interval by listing its counted dates.

Native desktop Excel 16.0 build 5569 executed the worksheet formulas in this example. The exclusive result was September 11 and the inclusive result September 9. Weekend-start, negative-offset, custom-weekend, zero-offset, fractional-offset and year-end controls also matched their expected dates. These are formula-engine checks on synthetic dates, not a verified regional holiday calendar or a recording of ribbon-menu actions.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does WORKDAY count the start date?**

A: For a positive offset, it counts eligible dates after the start. For a positive task duration that includes the first eligible date on or after the start, use WORKDAY(start-1,days,holidays) and verify that this matches your business rule.

**Q: Why is my holiday not being excluded?**

A: Check that the holiday cell is a real numeric Excel date, the correct calendar date, and inside the referenced range. Also check the copied formula did not move the range. WORKDAY does not automatically know your country’s public holidays.

**Q: Can WORKDAY calculate the number of business days between two dates?**

A: WORKDAY calculates a resulting date from an offset. A between-dates count uses NETWORKDAYS or NETWORKDAYS.INTL, whose endpoint rules must be considered separately. Do not confuse a three-day offset after a start with a duration that includes that start.

- [Worked example](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/excel-workday-holidays/example.csv)
- [workday-calendar-example.txt](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/excel-workday-holidays/workday-calendar-example.txt)

```text
A1: start_date
B1: workdays
C1: deadline
H1: excluded_dates
A2: =DATE(2026,9,4)
B2: 3
H2: =DATE(2026,9,7)
H3: =DATE(2026,9,10)
C2: =WORKDAY(A2,B2,$H$2:$H$3)
Format A2, C2, H2:H3 as yyyy-mm-dd.
Expected C2: 2026-09-11

```

# Unpivot Month Columns in Power Query: Keep IDs, Zeros, and a Clear Blank Rule

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-unpivot-month-columns
**Category:** file-conversion
**Description:** Turn monthly Excel columns into product-month rows with Power Query. Choose growing or fixed month columns and verify missing values, zeros, and totals.

## Summary
For a source containing only identifier columns plus monthly amounts, select the identifier columns and choose Unpivot Other Columns. New month columns then join the transformation on refresh. Decide how blanks should behave first: unpivot omits null values, while numeric zero must remain a real observation.

A monthly export may add another column every month, making filters, charts, and comparisons harder to maintain. Unpivot changes that layout into one month column and one amount column while repeating the product fields beside each value.

## Worked example

```csv
product,region,2026-01,2026-02,2026-03
P100,North,10,,0
P200,South,5,,8
P300,East,,,

```

**Expected:** After treating empty monthly fields as null, the output has four product-month rows totaling 23. P100 has January 10 and March 0; P200 has January 5 and March 8. P300 has no non-null monthly values and does not appear. Sort by product and month for the displayed order.

### Define the row that the output should represent

The input contains three products and three month columns. One output row should represent one product, one region, and one month with a recorded amount. Keep product and region together as identifiers; neither belongs in the amount column.

Use year-month headings such as 2026-01 rather than January alone. They distinguish years and sort chronologically as text when consistently padded. Remove worksheet totals and commentary columns before importing the sample. Otherwise, an unpivot of all non-identifier columns could mistake them for months.

**Figure: Wide months become individual observations**

Synthetic example with missing February excluded and recorded zero retained.

The product’s missing February creates no output row, while March zero remains a product-month observation.

One source row:
P100 | North
2026-01: 10
2026-02: missing
2026-03: 0

Two output rows:
P100 | North | 2026-01 | 10
P100 | North | 2026-03 | 0

### Build a refreshable unpivot in desktop Excel

This walkthrough targets desktop Excel on Windows with Power Query. Enter the source in A1:E4, with blank cells for the missing monthly values. Create an Excel Table with headers and name it MonthlySales. The sample is intentionally small enough to inspect every resulting row.

- Click inside MonthlySales and choose Data > From Table/Range to open Power Query Editor. Keep product and region as Text.
- Inspect the month columns. The blank worksheet cells should appear as null. If an upstream source provides empty text instead, normalize that to null before applying the numeric type.
- Set the three amount columns to Decimal Number. Review any conversion errors; do not remove error rows to force a matching row count.
- Select product and region together, right-click a selected header, and choose Unpivot Other Columns. Rename Attribute to month and Value to amount.
- Sort product ascending, then month ascending. Confirm the four expected observations, then choose Home > Close & Load to a new worksheet.

### Choose how future columns will be handled

Use Unpivot Other Columns when product and region are the complete set of fixed identifiers and every other column is a monthly amount. If you later add 2026-04, it becomes another month on refresh, provided that it is inside MonthlySales.

For a fixed report covering only January through March, choose Unpivot Only Selected Columns on those three month headers. A subsequently added April column stays outside that specific unpivot operation. Do not assume the plain Unpivot Columns command always means a permanently fixed list; inspect the generated step and choose the explicit option that matches your rule.

| Source change | Unpivot Other Columns | Unpivot Only Selected Columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add April amount column | April becomes month rows | April is not unpivoted |
| Add owner metadata column | Owner is unpivoted unless protected or removed | Owner remains a separate column |
| Need a fixed Jan–Mar extract | Requires an explicit month restriction | Choose the three month columns |
| Add more product rows | Processes new rows within the source | Processes new rows within the source |

### Use an explicit empty-value policy

A null monthly value represents no recorded observation in this example. Table.Unpivot omits null entries; a product with only null monthly values therefore disappears from the long result. That is why P300 is absent. An empty text value is a different value, so normalize it deliberately instead of depending on an import’s guessing.

Zero means a recorded amount of zero and must remain. Replacing missing values with zero would create five additional observations in this sample. The total would still be 23, but the observation count would rise from four to nine and averages would change. An unchanged total is not proof that the missing-value policy is correct.

If a downstream system needs every product-month pair, retain a product-and-month scaffold and join recorded amounts to it, leaving absent amounts null. That is a different output contract from this sparse observation list; do not silently substitute zeros.

**Figure: Same total, different meaning**

Synthetic comparison showing why totals alone cannot validate a blank policy.

Replacing five missing entries with zeros changes the row count from four to nine despite leaving the sum unchanged.

Missing values omitted:
4 recorded observations
Total: 23
P300 absent

Missing replaced by zero:
9 observations
Total: 23
P300 appears three times

### Inspect or reuse the complete query

The query below reads the named Excel Table, changes empty monthly text to null, converts monthly amounts using an explicit culture, unpivots the non-key columns, and sorts the result. It assumes every non-key header is a month and amounts are compatible with the declared numeric convention.

To use it, create MonthlySales as described, then replace the query in Home > Advanced Editor. If your source also contains owner, total, or notes columns, remove or explicitly protect them first. Review the query after a schema change; accepting any new column is convenient only when that column means another month.

```powerquery
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="MonthlySales"]}[Content],
    Keys = {"product", "region"},
    Months = List.Difference(Table.ColumnNames(Source), Keys),
    EmptyTextToNull = Table.TransformColumns(
        Source,
        List.Transform(Months, (columnName) =>
            {columnName, each if _ = "" then null else _, type any})
    ),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(
        EmptyTextToNull,
        List.Transform(Months, each {_, type number}),
        "en-US"
    ),
    Long = Table.UnpivotOtherColumns(Typed, Keys, "month", "amount"),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Long, {{"product", Order.Ascending}, {"month", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted
```

### Validate the first load and the next month

Compare the loaded rows with the expected file. January totals 15 and March totals 8, so the total is 23. Confirm that March zero for P100 remains and that there are no February rows under the chosen missing-value rule.

For a refresh check, add 2026-04 inside the source Table with amounts 2, 3, and 4 for P100, P200, and P300. The Other Columns workflow should then produce seven rows totaling 32; P300 appears once for April. If April stays as a separate wide column, inspect which unpivot operation was generated.

Keep the long output as a Table for later summaries. If a PivotTable reports stale totals after refresh, confirm its source includes the refreshed output and refresh that report too.

The supplied M query was executed through the native Power Query provider in desktop Excel 16.0 build 5569, using the named MonthlySales Table. It returned the exact four expected rows, including the real zero and no February observations. Adding April inside the Table and refreshing produced seven rows totaling 32, with P300 appearing once. Independent checks also confirmed that replacing missing values with zero changes the base count to nine while retaining total 23. This verifies the named-table query output; it does not record the graphical Editor clicks or test every Excel edition.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why did unpivot delete a product?**

A: A product with null in every selected month contributes no value rows. In this sample that is P300. If you need to show products without observations, preserve a separate complete product-month scaffold and join the observed amounts to it.

**Q: Will next month be included automatically?**

A: Unpivot Other Columns includes additional columns other than the protected identifiers. The new month must first be inside the source Table, and the query must refresh. A fixed Only Selected Columns operation does not automatically unpivot that new month.

**Q: Should I replace blanks with zero before unpivoting?**

A: Only when your data contract explicitly says a blank means a measured zero. Otherwise it changes the observation count and can distort averages. This example treats blanks as missing and retains real zero amounts.

# Power Query Left Anti Join: Find Missing Rows Without Losing Duplicates

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-left-anti-join-missing-rows
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Find items absent from another table with a Power Query left anti join. Keep duplicate requests, separate blank IDs, and verify exact text matches.

## Summary
Put the records you want to check on the left, the reference list on the right, and select Left Anti in the Merge dialog. Keep only valid IDs in the comparison, preserve repeated left-side requests, and sort the result explicitly. Run a separate reversed comparison if you also need reference items that were never requested.

A missing-item report should answer a precise question: which requested records have no matching item in the available list? A left anti join is a useful way to build that report, but its direction, key cleaning, and duplicate policy determine what the answer actually means.

## Worked example

```csv
line_id,item_id,quantity
L1,A100,2
L2,A200,1
L3,A200,3
L4,A300,4
L5,,5
L6, A100,6

```

**Expected:** Of six requested rows, L5 has a missing key and is kept in a separate exception file. Among the five valid-key rows, L1 and L4 match the reference. The missing-row output contains L2, L3, and L6, with quantities totaling 10. L6 has a leading space, so its exact text key differs from A100.

### Define missing records, not just missing values

This procedure is for desktop Excel on Windows with Power Query. The requested list contains two requests for A200, identified by L2 and L3. Both represent real lines, so both should remain if A200 is absent from AvailableItems. A report of distinct missing item IDs would have a different grain and needs a separate deduplication step after the line-level comparison.

The reference list includes A300 twice. Those repeated entries do not change the existence question: L4 has at least one match. We also include A900 only on the right to show the direction of the operation. A left anti result cannot tell you about that right-only item. It answers what is absent from the right for the selected left records.

**Figure: Direction changes the question**

Illustrative exact-key comparison: left anti preserves unmatched left records; reversing the inputs answers a different question.

Illustrative exact-key comparison: left anti preserves unmatched left records; reversing the inputs answers a different question.

Requests compared to availability:
A200 lines L2 and L3 missing
Leading-space A100 line L6 missing

Availability compared to requests:
A900 never requested
Duplicate A300 still has a match

### Load both sources with a key policy

Create RequestedItems from requested-items.csv and AvailableItems from available-items.csv using Excel Tables with headers. Import each through Data > From Table/Range. Keep item_id as Text and line_id as Text. An item code is a label; converting 00123 to number 123 would change the comparison before the join begins.

Separate the empty-key request L5 before merging. This guide treats null, empty text, and whitespace-only text as invalid keys. They are not confirmed missing inventory items. Use an exception query or retain those rows in a separate table. For valid keys we deliberately keep surrounding whitespace, so the leading-space L6 remains a visible mismatch instead of being silently repaired.

### Create the left anti result

In each query, apply the agreed invalid-key filter. The supplied complete M query implements this rule explicitly. The graphical steps below assume the valid-key versions are already available as connection-only queries. Keep the raw Tables unchanged so you can trace an unexpected exclusion.

- Open the valid RequestedItems query and choose Home > Merge Queries > Merge Queries as New.
- Select valid AvailableItems as the second query. Click item_id in both previews and choose Left Anti as the join kind. Leave fuzzy matching off.
- Confirm the merge. Remove the nested right_matches or AvailableItems column; this report needs the left fields, so expanding right-side details adds no information.
- Keep line_id, item_id, and quantity. Sort by line_id ascending to obtain L2, L3, and L6 in the displayed order.
- Load to a new worksheet and compare every row with missing-items-expected.csv. Keep invalid-key-expected.csv separate from this business result.

### Use a complete query when the filter needs to be explicit

The following query reads the two named Excel Tables and preserves valid keys exactly as supplied. Text.Trim is used only to decide whether a key contains anything besides whitespace. It does not replace the key used for matching. That is why L6 still differs from A100 after filtering.

Create a blank query, open Home > Advanced Editor, and replace its contents with this code after making the two source Tables. The result contains unmatched valid request lines only. Build a separate reference to the raw requests for invalid IDs if you need that exception output on every refresh. The attached file documents the one invalid record in this example.

```powerquery
let
    Left = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="RequestedItems"]}[Content],
    Right = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="AvailableItems"]}[Content],
    LeftTyped = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Left, {{"line_id", type text}, {"item_id", type text}, {"quantity", Int64.Type}}),
    RightTyped = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Right, {{"item_id", type text}}),
    ValidLeft = Table.SelectRows(LeftTyped, each [item_id] <> null and Text.Trim([item_id]) <> ""),
    ValidRight = Table.SelectRows(RightTyped, each [item_id] <> null and Text.Trim([item_id]) <> ""),
    Missing = Table.NestedJoin(ValidLeft, {"item_id"}, ValidRight, {"item_id"}, "right_matches", JoinKind.LeftAnti),
    Output = Table.RemoveColumns(Missing, {"right_matches"}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Output, {{"line_id", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted
```

### Choose whether cleaning should change the answer

If your item specification says leading and trailing spaces are accidental, create a normalized comparison column in both queries with Text.Trim before matching. Keep the original item_id for audit. Under that revised rule, L6 matches A100 and disappears from the missing result; only L2 and L3 remain, totaling 4. Changing the normalization rule is a substantive change to the report, not a formatting improvement.

For keys defined by multiple fields, such as warehouse and item_id, select both fields in the same order in each preview. First ensure you have the same types and conventions on both sides. A match in the wrong warehouse is still missing from the requested warehouse. Conversely, adding line_id to the key is inappropriate if the reference list never claims to contain request-line identifiers.

**Figure: Audit the row partition**

Synthetic counts change only after an explicit rule allows whitespace normalization.

Synthetic counts change only after an explicit rule allows whitespace normalization.

Six input requests:
1 invalid key: L5
2 matched rows: L1, L4
3 missing rows: L2, L3, L6

With agreed trimming:
1 invalid key: L5
3 matched rows: L1, L4, L6
2 missing rows: L2, L3

### Check counts and reverse the comparison deliberately

The row partition is a strong first-load check: one invalid row plus two matched rows plus three unmatched rows equals the six inputs. Duplicate A200 lines remain distinct because line_id identifies the request. A count of distinct item IDs would not reconcile in the same way. Keep both counts if the report needs both workload and product coverage.

For the reverse report, use valid AvailableItems on the left and valid RequestedItems on the right with the same exact-key rules. The result is A900. If A900 appeared three times in the reference, a row-level reverse comparison would retain those three unmatched records; deduplicate only if the desired result is a list of unique reference IDs. Save the two reports with names that describe their direction.

The supplied M query was executed through the native Power Query provider in desktop Excel 16.0 build 5569. It returned L2, L3 and L6 exactly, totaling 10. An explicitly trimmed variant returned L2 and L3 totaling 4; a reversed variant returned A900. The six-row partition and separate invalid-key file were independently checked. These are named-table query-engine tests with synthetic inputs, not a recording of Merge dialog clicks or a guarantee about every source connector.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does left anti remove duplicates from my first table?**

A: No. It keeps each unmatched left record. L2 and L3 both remain because both request A200 and neither finds a matching reference key.

**Q: Why does an ID that looks present remain missing?**

A: Check data types, spaces, letter case, and all parts of a composite key. This sample intentionally retains a leading space to show the difference between exact and normalized matching.

**Q: Should blank IDs be called missing items?**

A: This guide separates them as invalid-key exceptions. An unidentified request is not sufficient evidence that a particular inventory item is unavailable.

# Power Query Promote Headers: Skip Report Titles Without Losing the First Record

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-promote-headers
**Category:** csv-structure
**Description:** Fix the wrong header row in Power Query. Remove a fixed report preamble, promote headers once, preserve text IDs, and check refresh changes.

## Summary
Return to the parsed raw rows before automatic header promotion or type conversion. Remove only the agreed preamble rows, promote the next row once, then assign types. In the sample, remove two report rows so item_id, region, and quantity become the headers, while all three inventory records remain.

A CSV export may begin with a report title and a preparation date before its actual table. Power Query can mistake that preamble for the column names, leaving the real headers in the data or consuming the first record. Correcting the step order is safer than renaming whatever columns happen to appear.

## Worked example

```csv
Warehouse export,,
Prepared 2026-09-13,,
item_id,region,quantity
0007,North,4
0012,South,0
0012,East,6

```

**Expected:** The six physical CSV records become one header row and three data rows after removing two report rows. IDs 0007 and 0012 remain text, including two legitimate 0012 records in different regions. Quantities total 10, and the zero record remains present.

### Find the true header row in the source

This walkthrough uses Power Query in Excel for Windows to import a comma-delimited UTF-8 file. The first source row contains a report title, and the second contains preparation metadata. The third is the actual header. Every source record contains three fields, so structural parsing can succeed while the chosen headings are still wrong.

Read the raw file or preview before changing the query. A line containing a plausible word such as quantity is useful evidence, but it is not a universal header-detection algorithm. For this export, the contract says there are exactly two preamble records followed by three known headings. That bounded rule lets us explain every removed row and detect a future layout change.

**Figure: Remove the report wrapper before promotion**

Illustrative row accounting: two preamble rows are removed and the third row becomes column names, leaving three records.

Illustrative row accounting: two preamble rows are removed and the third row becomes column names, leaving three records.

Six source records:
1 report title
2 prepared date
3 item_id,region,quantity
4-6 inventory records

Four table records:
item_id, region, quantity
0007 | North | 4
0012 | South | 0
0012 | East | 6

### Inspect automatic steps before adding new ones

Use Data > From Text/CSV and choose Transform Data. Check Applied Steps for Promoted Headers and Changed Type. If a previous step already promoted Warehouse export, a later Remove Top Rows operation is starting from the wrong row count. Work from the parsed Source step that still shows the original preamble as rows.

On a copy of the query, remove the inappropriate automatic promotion and any dependent type step, or edit the chain so the raw parsed table is the input to the correction. Inspect the preview immediately afterwards. It should have generic column names such as Column1 and show Warehouse export in its first row. Do not repeatedly promote headers until the column names look acceptable; each promotion consumes another row.

### Remove two rows and promote exactly once

The procedure assumes the raw Source preview still contains all six CSV records. If it does not, first identify where records have already been consumed. The source file remains unchanged throughout the transformation.

- In Power Query Editor, select Home > Remove Rows > Remove Top Rows and enter 2. The first remaining row must read item_id, region, quantity.
- Choose Use First Row as Headers from the Home or Transform tab. Confirm the three column names match the agreed labels exactly.
- Set item_id and region to Text; set quantity to Whole Number. Remove any earlier type conversion that would already have stripped the zero prefixes.
- Confirm the first data record is 0007, North, 4. If the first record shown is 0012, South, 0, the query may have promoted one row too many.
- Load the result to a new worksheet. Compare the output to headers-expected.csv, including the repeated item ID in a different region and the zero quantity.

### Use a complete query that rejects a moved or changed header

Download headers-input.csv to a local folder. Create a blank query, open Advanced Editor, paste the following program and replace FilePath with your actual local file path. It reads raw CSV records without automatic type detection, skips exactly two records and checks the complete header row before promotion. The required names and order are deliberately fixed for this export.

The header guard rejects an added preamble line, duplicate or empty heading and reordered headings. The parser uses exactly three columns with ExtraValues.Error so a fourth field is rejected rather than silently dropped. This program does not infer the new schema. A header-only export returns zero data rows; a file ending before the expected header returns an error. Quantity conversion errors remain errors to investigate, rather than rows to discard.

```powerquery
let
    FilePath = "C:\CSVInput\headers-input.csv",
    Raw = Csv.Document(File.Contents(FilePath), 3, ",", ExtraValues.Error, 65001),
    AfterPreamble = Table.Skip(Raw, 2),
    ExpectedHeaders = {"item_id", "region", "quantity"},
    Checked = if Table.RowCount(AfterPreamble) = 0 then error "Missing header row after the two-record preamble"
        else if Record.FieldValues(AfterPreamble{0}) <> ExpectedHeaders then error "Header contract changed: expected item_id,region,quantity"
        else AfterPreamble,
    Headers = Table.PromoteHeaders(Checked, [PromoteAllScalars=true]),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Headers, {{"item_id", type text}, {"region", type text}, {"quantity", Int64.Type}}, "en-US")
in
    Typed
```

### Handle duplicate or empty header labels as a schema problem

Power Query table column names must be unique, so promotion can disambiguate repeated labels by adding a suffix. That prevents a naming collision but does not explain which business field each repeated heading represents. If a source arrives with quantity twice, stop and ask which measure each column is intended to contain before mapping it into a stable report.

For this workflow, all three headings must be nonempty and exactly match the expected set. A blank heading or an extra field is a contract change to investigate, rather than a reason to silently use Column4. Trimming header whitespace may be an agreed repair, but retain a record of the original header text and check that trimming does not collapse two distinct headings into one name.

### Separate preamble changes from record changes

Adding a fourth inventory record below the header should be a routine refresh. Adding an extra report-title row above the header is different: a fixed Remove Top Rows of two will now promote the wrong line. Use the negative test in header-refresh-tests.txt to make sure the next operator recognizes this failure instead of manually deleting a data row.

For variable-length reports, choose a documented marker or a separate clean export format. A robust marker rule must address missing markers, multiple matches, and lines that resemble headings inside the data. Do not replace the simple fixed rule with a search for the first nonblank row; report titles are often nonblank too. If the source owner can provide a table-only CSV, that is easier to operate than inferring a changing presentation layout.

**Figure: Two refresh changes need different responses**

Illustrative comparison: growing data is expected; a moving header is a source-layout change that needs inspection.

Illustrative comparison: growing data is expected; a moving header is a source-layout change that needs inspection.

Add one data record:
Same three headers
One extra inventory row
Normal transformation

Add one preamble record:
Header moves down
Fixed skip is now wrong
Review the layout contract

### Protect the first record and the meaning of types

A useful check is to pin the first expected record by its full values. In this sample, 0007, North, 4 must survive every step. A correct total is not sufficient: losing one record and duplicating another could hide behind an unchanged sum. Check row count, first record, zero presence, and the two separate 0012 region records.

When the headings are numeric dates or other scalar values, Table.PromoteHeaders supports options that control promotion and culture. Avoid relying on how a local machine formats a date to construct a permanent column name. This example deliberately uses stable text headings. For monthly date headers, normalize the names to an agreed format before downstream steps refer to them.

### Keep a compact refresh checklist beside the query

Record the source filename pattern, comma delimiter, UTF-8 encoding, two-row preamble, exact header set, and identifier type. The file headers-contract.txt contains that information for the worked example. It also states that duplicate item IDs are allowed across regions, so a later operator does not remove them to make the data appear unique.

At the next refresh, compare the first preview records before loading the full report. After loading, confirm that the new row count agrees with the expected source inventory records and that quantity conversion produced no errors. If the export begins including totals at the bottom, treat that as a new contract decision; this guide has no footer rule and should not silently count a report total as another inventory record.

### Reproduce the checked result

The downloadable query was executed in the native Power Query engine through Excel 16.0 build 5569.0 on October 5, 2026. The three output records matched headers-expected.csv exactly: 0007/North/4, 0012/South/0 and 0012/East/6. Adding 0020/West/3 produced four records totaling 13.

Native tests also rejected a moved header, duplicate heading, blank heading, extra field and missing header. A header-only file returned zero records, and a nonnumeric quantity stayed identifiable as a conversion error. These checks exercise parsing and M execution; they do not claim that every version uses identical automatic import steps or menu labels. Inspect your own Source and Applied Steps before using the menu-only route.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why is my first data row missing?**

A: A header promotion consumes the first row of its input. Inspect whether headers were promoted automatically and then promoted again after the real header was already in place.

**Q: Can I just rename Column1 and Column2?**

A: Renaming is suitable when the source truly has no header row. If the real header is still among the data, renaming alone leaves that row in your records and may cause type errors.

**Q: Will this work if the report title grows to three rows?**

A: The fixed two-row rule must be revised. Detect and review the changed preamble, or use a well-defined marker rule that also handles missing and duplicate markers.

# Power Query Split Column into Rows: Keep IDs, Order, and Empty-Token Rules

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/power-query-split-column-into-rows
**Category:** text-cleanup
**Description:** Split semicolon-separated tags into Power Query rows with repeated IDs, token positions, blank handling, and an auditable six-row result.

## Summary
In Power Query Editor, select the text field, choose Split Column > By Delimiter, select each occurrence of the separator, and choose Rows under Advanced options. Trim the resulting tokens and remove empty tokens only under an explicit rule. Use the supplied query when you also need each token’s original position.

A tag field containing red; blue;red hides three entries inside one cell. Splitting into rows makes those entries filterable, but it also repeats the parent ID and may expose empty tokens or duplicate tags. Choose whether the output represents tag occurrences or unique ticket-tag relationships before removing anything.

## Worked example

```csv
ticket_id,tags
T1,red; blue;red
T2,green;;
T3,
T4, blue ; yellow 

```

**Expected:** The output contains six nonempty tag occurrences across T1, T2, and T4. T1 retains red twice at positions 1 and 3. T2 retains green and drops two empty tokens. T3 has no tag and contributes no output row. Leading and trailing token spaces are trimmed, while parent ticket IDs remain text.

### Choose occurrences or unique relationships

This example is for Excel on Windows with Power Query with local Table TicketTags. Each source row represents one ticket, and the ticket_id values are unique in this sample. The tag field uses a semicolon as a list separator. Semicolons are not allowed inside an individual tag, and the source has no quoting or escaping convention for literal separators.

Our output represents each nonempty tag occurrence. T1 has red, blue, and red again, so the duplicate red must remain. If your reporting question is how many tickets carry red, create a separate unique ticket-tag result after the occurrence table. Counting occurrence rows answers a different question and would count T1 twice for red. Keep the two outputs named clearly so later charts use the intended one.

**Figure: A repeated tag is still an occurrence**

Synthetic illustration: splitting repeats the parent ID and preserves two red occurrences with different positions.

Synthetic illustration: splitting repeats the parent ID and preserves two red occurrences with different positions.

One parent record:
T1
red; blue;red

Three child records:
T1 | 1 | red
T1 | 2 | blue
T1 | 3 | red

### Import and use the Rows option

Create an Excel Table named TicketTags from ticket-tags-input.csv, then use Data > From Table/Range. Set ticket_id and tags to Text. Inspect the delimiter inside the tags field; it is a semicolon even though the outer CSV file is separated by commas. These are two distinct parsing stages.

- Select tags and choose Transform > Split Column > By Delimiter. Use Custom if necessary and enter a semicolon.
- Select Each occurrence of the delimiter. Open Advanced options and choose Rows, then confirm. Choosing Columns would instead produce a growing set of tag columns.
- Select the split tag field and choose Transform > Format > Trim. This example removes leading and trailing whitespace from individual tokens.
- Filter the resulting field to exclude null and empty text according to the declared no-tag rule. Retain the parent ticket_id alongside every surviving token.
- Rename the token column tag and load a new worksheet. This menu workflow creates the relationship rows; use the complete query below if original token positions are required.

### Decide what happens to empty tokens and empty parents

T2 contains green followed by two separators, which describes green plus two empty token positions. The report keeps only meaningful tags, so those empty tokens are removed. T3 has no tag field value and produces no child record. Preserve the original ticket Table if another report must still count all four tickets, including tickets without tags.

Do not fill an empty tag with the preceding tag. That would create extra classifications that the source never supplied. If an empty token signals a malformed export rather than an acceptable omission, keep an exception report before filtering. The attached token-audit.txt gives the expected empty-token counts for this particular sample; no universal empty-token policy is implied.

### Preserve token positions with the complete query

The query uses Text.Split for the simple semicolon convention, constructs a position before filtering, and expands each remaining record. tag_position therefore records the original token slot, not a new consecutive sequence after empty values are discarded. A value such as red;;blue would produce positions 1 and 3. That makes gaps visible when the source list needs auditing. It removes empty token lists before expansion so the no-tag policy does not depend on how the engine represents an expanded empty list.

Create the TicketTags source Table first. In a blank query, open Advanced Editor and insert the following code. It keeps ticket_id unchanged and sorts the output by ticket_id and original position for the downloadable expected result. If the input later contains repeated parent ticket IDs, add a source-row identifier too; ticket_id plus token position would no longer uniquely identify an occurrence.

```powerquery
let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="TicketTags"]}[Content],
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source, {{"ticket_id", type text}, {"tags", type text}}),
    WithRecords = Table.AddColumn(Typed, "tokens", each
        let
            Parts = if [tags] = null then {} else Text.Split([tags], ";"),
            Records = List.Transform(List.Positions(Parts), (i) => [tag_position = i + 1, tag = Text.Trim(Parts{i})])
        in List.Select(Records, each [tag] <> "")
    ),
    NonemptyParents = Table.SelectRows(WithRecords, each List.Count([tokens]) > 0),
    ExpandedList = Table.ExpandListColumn(NonemptyParents, "tokens"),
    ExpandedRecord = Table.ExpandRecordColumn(ExpandedList, "tokens", {"tag_position", "tag"}),
    Output = Table.SelectColumns(ExpandedRecord, {"ticket_id", "tag_position", "tag"}),
    OutputTypes = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Output, {{"tag_position", Int64.Type}, {"tag", type text}}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(OutputTypes, {{"ticket_id", Order.Ascending}, {"tag_position", Order.Ascending}})
in
    Sorted
```

### Avoid accidental multiplication of unrelated fields

When one row expands into several tag rows, other parent columns are repeated. If you later include ticket_cost of 100 on T1, all three T1 rows could show 100. Summing that child table would report 300 for the same parent cost. Keep parent-level measures in a separate ticket table or define an explicit allocation policy before summing them at tag level.

Similarly, splitting two independent list columns one after the other can create combinations. A ticket with two tags and three assignees may produce six rows if both lists are expanded independently. Do not assume the first tag belongs with the first assignee unless the source specification defines positional pairing. This guide expands one list only and does not infer relationships between separate lists.

**Figure: Keep the parent denominator separately**

Illustrative row counts: a child table omits tagless tickets and counts occurrences rather than total tickets.

Illustrative row counts: a child table omits tagless tickets and counts occurrences rather than total tickets.

Source ticket table:
4 tickets
T3 has no tags

Tag occurrence table:
6 rows
3 represented tickets
T1 red occurs twice

### Know when this separator rule is too simple

Text.Split treats every semicolon as a boundary. If a tag itself can contain a semicolon, the source needs an escaping or quoting specification and an appropriate parser. Do not apply this query to a full CSV record as a replacement for CSV parsing. Outer CSV quotation rules and an inner list field require separate handling.

For the worked sample, verify six rows, three represented ticket IDs, and the exact positions listed in ticket-tags-expected.csv. A refresh test of T5 with red;;blue should add two rows at positions 1 and 3. T6 with a whitespace-only tags value should add none. Keep an audit count of omitted parents if downstream coverage reporting depends on every source ticket being represented.

### Check the native result before reusing the query

On October 5, 2026, the exact downloadable M query was executed through the native Power Query engine in Excel 16.0 build 5569.0. All six rows matched ticket-tags-expected.csv, including both red occurrences on T1 and the absence of T3. The result represented three tickets and five distinct ticket-tag pairs.

Additional native cases checked red;;blue at positions 1 and 3, null, empty text and whitespace-only lists, and repeated parent IDs. Empty parents contributed no child record; repeated IDs retained separate occurrences. The query sorts by ticket_id and position, so it does not preserve original parent-row ordering when IDs are repeated. Add a source-row identifier and sort by that identifier if source-row order matters. Menu clicks and all Excel versions were not exercised.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why did my ticket count increase after splitting?**

A: The output counts tag occurrences. Parent IDs repeat for each retained token, so use the original ticket table or distinct parent IDs when you need a ticket count.

**Q: Should repeated tags be removed?**

A: Only for a unique ticket-tag report. This guide preserves occurrences, including both red entries on T1; a separate deduplicated report would contain five relationships.

**Q: Does the query understand quoted semicolons inside a tag?**

A: No. Its contract forbids semicolons inside a tag. Use a parser that matches the actual source escaping convention if literal separators are allowed.

# Google Sheets SUMIF Wildcards: Match Text or a Literal Asterisk

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-sumif-wildcards-literal-text
**Category:** numbers-identifiers
**Description:** Use Google Sheets SUMIF for starts-with, contains and literal asterisk matching. Compare worked totals and use equality for punctuation-bearing product codes.

## Summary
In a SUMIF text criterion, * matches zero or more characters and ? matches one character. Use ~* for a literal star and ~? for a literal question mark. In this sample, "SKU*" totals 220 but "SKU~*" totals 10. For exact product codes containing punctuation, use the tested equality formula below instead of assuming every escape behaves as expected.

A product code containing an asterisk can accidentally match many more products than intended. The same SUMIF syntax that is useful for a starts-with report needs an escape when the star is part of the actual code.

## Worked example

```csv
code,amount
SKU*,10
SKU?,20
SKU-A,30
SKU-AB,40
SKU~,50
OTHER,60
SKU,70
```

**Expected:** The starts-with criterion SKU* totals 220, while literal SKU* totals only 10. SKU-? selects SKU-A for 30 and excludes SKU-AB. All source amounts total 280, including OTHER at 60.

### Separate pattern matching from literal code matching

Put sumif-patterns-input.csv in A1:B8 in desktop Google Sheets. Every code is text and every amount is numeric. The code SKU* genuinely contains a star; it is not a placeholder in the input. Keep the complete fixture, because the similar-looking codes are what expose an overbroad criterion.

The intended report determines whether the star is a wildcard. A manager asking for the whole SKU family wants 220. A reconciliation asking for the specific code printed as SKU* wants 10. Both requests are reasonable, and the same visible characters in a criterion cell can produce very different results unless the distinction is explicit.

### Start with the three wildcard meanings

An asterisk matches zero or more characters, so SKU* includes the plain code SKU as well as its longer variants. A question mark stands for one character, so SKU-? matches SKU-A but not SKU-AB. The tilde is the escape prefix used when a wildcard character should be treated literally.

Enter the three formulas below in separate summary cells. They must return 220, 30 and 70. The last result is a useful control: the exact text SKU is a real record, and the asterisk pattern includes that record because zero extra characters are allowed. Do not mistake starts-with for starts-with-and-has-a-suffix.

```text
Starts with SKU: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU*",B2:B8)
Exactly one character after SKU-: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU-?",B2:B8)
Exact SKU: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU",B2:B8)
```

**Figure: One star can select a whole family**

Illustrative synthetic distinction between wildcard and literal product-code matching.

Pattern criterion SKU*; SKU*, SKU?, SKU-A; SKU-AB, SKU~, SKU; Total: 220; Literal criterion SKU~*; Only the code SKU*; Total: 10

Pattern criterion SKU*:
SKU*, SKU?, SKU-A
SKU-AB, SKU~, SKU
Total: 220

Literal criterion SKU~*:
Only the code SKU*
Total: 10

### Escape literal stars and question marks; check tildes separately

Use ~* for a literal star and ~? for a literal question mark. The criterion still needs quotes when written directly in a formula. SKU~* totals 10 and SKU~? totals 20 in the worked Sheet. To find a literal star anywhere, combine a wildcard, an escaped star and a final wildcard: *~** also totals 10.

Google’s SUMIF documentation describes ~~ as the escape for a literal tilde. In our actual browser Sheet on October 5, 2026, however, SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU~~",B2:B8) returned 0, while the plain "SKU~" criterion returned 50. That is an observed result for this fixture, not a promise about every workbook or a diagnosed product defect. The downloadable expected-pattern file therefore covers the verified star/question-mark cases. Use the equality method below for a literal punctuation-bearing code.

```text
Literal SKU*: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU~*",B2:B8)
Literal SKU?: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"SKU~?",B2:B8)
Contains a literal star: =SUMIF(A2:A8,"*~**",B2:B8)
```

### Match a product-code cell with equality instead of wildcard criteria

Enter the exact requested product code in E2 and put the formula below in F2. This compares each source code with E2 directly; punctuation is part of the value, not a SUMIF pattern. SKU*, SKU? and SKU~ return 10, 20 and 50 respectively, and SKU-A returns 30.

This example requires numeric, error-free amounts in B2:B8 and the same row bounds in both ranges. Check them with ISNUMBER before calculating. Use bounded ranges rather than whole columns. Equality is case-insensitive here; this formula does not promise a case-sensitive code lookup. It also sums every matching occurrence, so duplicate source codes need an explicit business policy rather than automatic removal.

```text
=SUMPRODUCT(($A$2:$A$8=E2)*$B$2:$B$8)
```

### Keep numeric totals separate from matching text

Check =ISNUMBER(B2) down the amount column. A code matching the criterion does not guarantee that its amount is usable numeric data. Preserve negative adjustments if they belong in the report; dropping a refund can make a technically correct pattern produce a misleading business total.

Use text wildcards for text labels, not for month numbers displayed by formatted date cells. Dates can be stored numerically even when they look like text. A request such as January sales needs date boundaries with a year, not an assumption that a date's printed 01 prefix is searchable text. The existing date guides cover that separate workflow.

As a separate acceptance exercise, append SKU* with -3 and SKU* with 0 below the sample and extend both ranges to row 10. The SKU* wildcard total becomes 217; literal SKU* equality becomes 7. Both added occurrences count, and the refund is retained. These two outcomes were calculated in the worked browser Sheet; keep the original A2:B8 bounds when reproducing the baseline downloads.

### Verify matched records, not only the final sum

For SKU-?, inspect the source and confirm that SKU-A is included and SKU-AB is excluded. For SKU*, confirm that OTHER is the only omitted row. For the literal star criterion, inspect the actual code cell rather than relying on a description such as star product that may hide its punctuation.

The fixture has positive, distinct amounts to make failures easy to see. In a real export, wrongly included positive and negative rows can cancel out and leave the same total. Keep a record-level sample with a known expected match set when changing criteria. A total is a useful reconciliation, but it is not a substitute for checking which rows were selected.

**Figure: A question mark matches one character**

Illustrative synthetic single-character wildcard boundary.

Included by SKU-?; SKU-A | 30; One character after hyphen; Excluded by SKU-?; SKU-AB | 40; Two characters after hyphen

Included by SKU-?:
SKU-A | 30
One character after hyphen

Excluded by SKU-?:
SKU-AB | 40
Two characters after hyphen

### Choose a different tool when the requirement changes

SUMIF provides one matching criterion. A report that also requires a specific region, status or date interval needs a deliberately constructed multi-condition calculation. Do not concatenate unrelated business fields into the product code merely to fit everything into a single wildcard.

The examples use English function names and comma separators in Google Sheets. SUMIF wildcards are not regular expressions: a dot or bracket does not acquire regex meaning. The worked formulas were entered and calculated in an actual browser Sheet on October 5, 2026, including the six supported pattern totals and the four literal-code equality totals. Check the source types and matched records again when adapting the example.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why does SKU* total much more than the SKU* row?**

A: The star is a wildcard in the criterion. Use SKU~* when the star is part of the literal code.

**Q: How do I match a tilde itself?**

A: Google documents ~~ as the literal-tilde escape, but it returned 0 for SKU~ in our worked Sheet while equality returned the intended 50. For this product-code task, use the supplied SUMPRODUCT equality formula and verify its matched rows.

**Q: Can I use January wildcard text on real dates?**

A: Do not infer text content from a date display. Use actual date boundaries for a dated report, including the year.
