# Google Sheets QUERY Missing Values: Repair Mixed Text and Number Columns

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-query-mixed-data-types
**Category:** numbers-identifiers
**Description:** Find why QUERY drops text or numeric IDs, then normalize an identifier column without turning amounts into text. Includes typed fixtures and expected results.

## Summary
QUERY chooses one data type for each column from the majority of its values; minority types become null for the query. For an identifier such as a room code, build a separate text helper column and query that. Keep quantities numeric, specify the header count, and verify that conversion preserves the identifiers you intended.

A QUERY report can show a room name as blank even though the source cell is populated. Adding more rows can change which values disappear. This often happens when one identifier column contains both numbers and text.

## Worked example

```csv
booking_id,room,hours
B01,101,2
B02,102,3
B03,Studio-A,4
B04,103,1
B05,Studio-B,5
```

**Expected:** The repaired report preserves all five booking IDs, all five room labels and 15 total hours. A text criterion for Studio-A returns B03 with four hours. The types companion is essential because a CSV cannot encode the Google Sheets type of each cell.

### Reproduce mixed types deliberately

Put the booking fixture in A1:C6 in desktop Google Sheets. Set B2, B3 and B5 to numeric 101, 102 and 103; B4 and B6 are the text Studio-A and Studio-B. All C2:C6 values must be numbers. The companion types file describes the intended cell types and is a setup specification, not a second table to append to the bookings.

Put =ISNUMBER(B2) in D2 and fill it down through D6. The intended pattern is TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE. An import that made every room plain text will not reproduce the bug, even if it looks identical. Leave the room cells as mixed types for the diagnostic; changing only their number format does not turn them into text.

### Observe the raw query before changing it

Run the first formula in J1 on an otherwise empty area. With numeric values in the majority, the two Studio labels are the minority type. Inspect both those rows and their booking IDs. A select of every column can retain the row while showing a null room; a condition that requires a non-null room can also remove that row from the result.

The second formula makes that filtering consequence visible. B03 and B05 should be absent from this deliberately broken diagnostic report. The row loss comes from the additional where condition, so do not describe every mixed-type query as always deleting entire rows. Keep this test report separate from the repaired output.

For this exact fixture, J2:L6 contains five bookings and 15 hours, with blank room cells beside B03 and B05. N2:P4 contains only B01, B02 and B04, totaling six hours. The two raw expected CSVs encode the query nulls as empty fields, not the literal word null. They are diagnostic results to compare with, not repaired sources to import over A:C.

```text
J1: =QUERY(A1:C6,"select A,B,C",1)
N1: =QUERY(A1:C6,"select A,B,C where B is not null",1)
```

**Figure: Type inference changes the query view**

Illustrative query view of a synthetic column; the source cells themselves remain populated.

Original rooms; 101, 102, Studio-A; 103, Studio-B; Numeric-majority query; 101, 102, null; 103, null

Original rooms:
101, 102, Studio-A
103, Studio-B

Numeric-majority query:
101, 102, null
103, null

### Choose types according to meaning

A room identifier is a label, so text is appropriate even when one label contains digits only. Hours represent quantities, so converting that whole column to text would solve the wrong problem and complicate totals. Decide each column independently before building a helper table.

Leading zeroes require special care. If a source code 00101 was already imported as the number 101, converting it to text yields a representation of the stored number; it cannot infer how many zeroes the original had. Recover the original text or apply a documented fixed-width rule. Do not invent missing digits from the report.

### Build a visible normalized table

Use E1:G6 for the repaired source. Put booking_id, room_text and hours in E1:G1. Enter the three formulas below in row 2 and fill them down to row 6. Keep the original A:C beside it so every transformed room can be inspected directly. This modest helper-table approach is easier to maintain than hiding every conversion in a single long query.

Select B2:B6 and use Format > Number > Custom number format with the pattern 0 before building the helpers. This makes the numeric rooms display as integers without padding. TO_TEXT retains existing formatting: a padded or currency format can become part of the resulting identifier. The fixture expects 101, 102 and 103, so compare F2:F6 with the original values before continuing. The format changes display, not the mixed-type contract; TO_TEXT is the conversion step.

```text
E2: =A2
F2: =TO_TEXT(B2)
G2: =C2
```

### Query the text identifiers with explicit headers

Clear the earlier diagnostic output in J1:L6 after preserving it if needed. Run the repaired query in J1. The source includes one header row, so the last argument is 1. A header guess is unnecessary when you know the shape of your own table. The query references E, F and G because those are the actual helper-sheet columns.

To select Studio-A, use the second formula in a different empty area. The room comparison is now a text comparison and the query literal is enclosed in single quotes inside the formula string. This example uses a fixed synthetic label; constructing a query string from arbitrary user input needs separate escaping and is outside this procedure.

```text
J1: =QUERY(E1:G6,"select E,F,G where E is not null",1)
N1: =QUERY(E1:G6,"select E,F,G where F = 'Studio-A'",1)
```

### Reconcile identifiers as well as totals

Compare the repaired report with query-preserved-expected.csv. You need five bookings, five nonblank room labels and 15 hours. A correct total by itself is insufficient: a select-only query could retain the hours while blanking the corresponding room. Conversely, a count can be correct while one label has been reformatted incorrectly.

Check Studio-A and Studio-B explicitly after adding numeric-looking rooms. Because every helper room is text, the report no longer depends on whether the latest import contains more numeric or more alphabetic room codes. Preserve the source booking ID through the transformation so a discrepancy can be traced to one input row.

Place the checks below in R2:R4, outside both query outputs. They should return 5, 0 and 15 after the repair. COUNTBLANK checks the five expected room positions rather than relying on a total alone. This fixture has no empty booking IDs, no empty room labels and no source errors. If a real booking has a missing room, keep it visible for review; do not substitute a guessed label merely to make the blank count pass.

```text
R2: =COUNTA(J2:J6)
R3: =COUNTBLANK(K2:K6)
R4: =SUM(L2:L6)
```

**Figure: A complete reconciliation has three checks**

Illustrative checks for the synthetic repaired report; totals alone do not establish intact labels.

Required output; Bookings: 5; Nonblank rooms: 5; Hours: 15; Spot checks; B03 -> Studio-A -> 4; B05 -> Studio-B -> 5

Required output:
Bookings: 5
Nonblank rooms: 5
Hours: 15

Spot checks:
B03 -> Studio-A -> 4
B05 -> Studio-B -> 5

### Treat numeric data problems as a separate repair

If an amount column contains the text pending, turning all amounts into text is usually not an acceptable accounting rule. Separate valid numeric records from unresolved records and decide whether the report should stop, exclude with a visible count, or wait for correction. Replacing pending with zero silently changes the meaning of the data.

This guide addresses identifier preservation rather than grouped totals. Once types are consistent, the existing QUERY grouping guide can handle aggregation. Extend all helper formulas when adding rows, inspect any new format conventions and rerun the row-and-total reconciliation. The supplied validator checks the fixture contract; it does not reproduce the native QUERY engine or prove a particular import created the intended types.

### Verified practice results

This synthetic example was calculated in Google Sheets on October 11, 2026. The raw select returned five bookings with the two Studio room labels blank; adding the nonnull condition returned only B01, B02 and B04, totaling six hours. The text-helper repair returned all five complete labels and 15 hours, and the Studio-A query returned B03 with four hours.

Changing B03 from four to six hours recalculated the repaired total to 17 and the Studio-A result to six. Restoring the source restored the baseline. Typed source cells, formula results and these input changes were checked in the native calculation engine; the repaired result was also inspected in the browser. This does not verify every CSV import route, custom-format convention or spreadsheet locale. Use the source-type and reconciliation checks on your own imported data.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why did the report change after I added more records?**

A: Mixed columns depend on the majority type used by QUERY. A changing mixture can alter which values become null. Give identifier columns an explicit text representation before querying.

**Q: Does TO_TEXT recover leading zeroes lost during import?**

A: No. It converts the stored value using its formatting. Recover the original code from the source or use an independently documented width rule.

**Q: Should I convert every column to text?**

A: No. Text is appropriate for labels and codes; quantities and calculation dates need their own numeric type rules.

# Sort by Multiple Columns in Google Sheets: Keep Rows Together and Break Ties

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-sort-multiple-columns
**Category:** compare-combine
**Description:** Build a Google Sheets SORT formula with department, descending score and a final ID tie-breaker. Keep complete records together and verify exact row order.

## Summary
Pass the complete record range to SORT, followed by each key and its direction in priority order. For this example, sort department ascending, score descending and unique record ID ascending: =SORT(A2:D8,2,TRUE,3,FALSE,1,TRUE). Keep the original data and put the sorted view in a separate empty area.

Sorting a score column by itself can detach scores from their owners. Even when entire rows move together, equal scores leave the desired order unclear unless you decide the next comparison key.

## Worked example

```csv
record_id,department,score,owner
R03,Sales,90,Ada
R01,Support,80,Bea
R04,Sales,95,Cam
R02,Sales,90,Dee
R07,Support,80,Eli
R06,Sales,0,Fay
R05,Support,100,Gus
```

**Expected:** Department-first order is R04, R02, R03, R06, R05, R01, R07. All seven records and their owner-score associations are preserved. If score becomes the primary key, the separate expected file begins with Support record R05 at 100.

### Write the ordering rule before the formula

Use the desktop browser version of Google Sheets with English function names. The sample represents a review list, not a universal ranking policy. Department groups come first; within each department, higher scores appear first; equal scores are ordered by the unique record ID. An ID tie-breaker is an explicit display rule, not evidence that one person performed better.

This rule places every Sales record before every Support record even when a Support score is larger. That is intentional. If your actual requirement is a company-wide leaderboard, score should be the first key. The two expected downloads make this choice visible rather than hiding it in the order of formula arguments.

### Select the full record rectangle and leave headers out

Put sort-input.csv in A1:D8. Keep record_id, department, score and owner together in the source range. Copy the headers to F1:I1 and reserve F2:I8 for the formula result. The data-only input is A2:D8; including row 1 would ask the formula to sort the headers as data.

Put =ISNUMBER(C2) in E2 and fill it down through E8. All seven results must be TRUE, including the row containing zero. A numeric-looking text score should be corrected under a clear import rule before relying on the ordering. Keep E as a temporary type check outside the A:D record range; do not change all scores to text just to make the cells look consistent.

### Enter all sorting keys in priority order

Enter the formula below in F2. The first key is the second column of A:D, which is department. TRUE means ascending. The next key is the third column, score, with FALSE for descending. The final key is the first column, record_id, ascending. Each direction belongs to the key immediately before it.

These integer key positions are relative to the range passed to SORT. If the source rectangle later moves to B:E, department is still its second column even though it sits in worksheet column C. Recalculate the positions if you change which columns the formula returns. Keeping the source headers visible helps catch that distinction.

```text
F2: =SORT(A2:D8,2,TRUE,3,FALSE,1,TRUE)
```

**Figure: Sorting has an explicit hierarchy**

Illustrative synthetic ordering with a final ID tie-breaker for the two Sales records scoring 90.

Compare in this order; 1. Department ascending; 2. Score descending; 3. Record ID ascending; Sales result; R04 | 95; R02 | 90; R03 | 90; R06 | 0

Compare in this order:
1. Department ascending
2. Score descending
3. Record ID ascending

Sales result:
R04 | 95
R02 | 90
R03 | 90
R06 | 0

### Verify ties instead of assuming a stable order

R02 and R03 both belong to Sales and score 90. The final key puts R02 first despite R03 appearing earlier in the original input. R01 and R07 tie in Support at 80, and their IDs settle that order too. These cases verify the third key, which a dataset with no ties would never exercise.

Do not rely on an undocumented original-row order when all your named keys are equal. If preserving original sequence is the requirement, capture a unique sequence value in the source and use that as the final key. Freeze that value before any manual reordering; a live ROW-based formula can change when the source is rearranged.

### Change the primary key when the report question changes

For a score-first leaderboard, put the alternative below in K2 with headers in K1:N1. It orders score descending, department ascending and record ID ascending. R05 at 100 now appears before all Sales records. The same source data can support both reports because neither formula sorts the source in place.

Compare K2:N8 with sort-score-first-expected.csv. Keep the formula label explicit so someone does not mistake a grouped list for an overall ranking. Adding another key only resolves ties in earlier keys; it does not override a higher-priority key or compute a weighted score from several columns.

```text
K2: =SORT(A2:D8,3,FALSE,2,TRUE,1,TRUE)
```

**Figure: Primary-key choice changes the first row**

Illustrative comparison of two deliberate sorting policies using the same synthetic records.

Department first; R04 | Sales | 95; All Sales before Support; Score first; R05 | Support | 100; Highest score across teams

Department first:
R04 | Sales | 95
All Sales before Support

Score first:
R05 | Support | 100
Highest score across teams

### Keep manual notes attached to IDs

The sorted output can move whenever a source score changes. Typing a comment in the next unused column beside the output does not attach it to the record ID. After recalculation, that comment could sit beside a different person. Store notes in the source record or in a separate table keyed by record_id, then look them up.

Likewise, reserve the whole output rectangle for the formula. A note entered inside it can prevent expansion. If you need to hand off a fixed snapshot, copy the verified output to a separate tab and paste values there. Record when the snapshot was taken; it no longer recalculates with the source.

### Reconcile records and extend the range carefully

Compare the seven IDs in the source with the seven IDs in each output. Check R03 still belongs to Ada and R02 still belongs to Dee. The total score is 535 before and after sorting, but a matching total alone would not detect owners being detached from their scores. Verify both membership and associations.

When adding rows, extend the complete A:D rectangle and any external key ranges together. Blank department values, duplicate IDs, locale-specific collation and text scores need explicit policies before expanding the example to production. The independent validator checks the stated tuple ordering and record preservation. It does not run the native Sheets engine or establish how unspecified ties behave.

Enter the following checks in P2:P4; the expected values are 7, 535 and 1. P4 confirms that the real zero score survived. Read the complete F2:F8 ID order against sort-expected.csv, then check R02 with Dee and R03 with Ada. These arithmetic checks support the row comparison; they do not replace it or prove that each owner stayed attached to the correct score.

For real data, decide what a missing department or score means before sorting. The practice range contains neither, so it deliberately makes no promise about where blank keys should appear. Keep unresolved records in a visible review list or establish a documented category before expanding the range. If record IDs are not unique, add a unique, preserved sequence as the final key; adding a duplicate ID key cannot settle an otherwise complete tie.

```text
P2: =COUNTA(F2:F8)
P3: =SUM(H2:H8)
P4: =COUNTIF(H2:H8,0)
```

### Verified practice results

This synthetic example was calculated in Google Sheets on October 11, 2026. Both complete-row outputs matched their expected CSVs: department-first began R04, R02, R03, R06; score-first began R05, R04, R02, R03. All seven IDs retained their owners, the total stayed 535, and the zero score remained.

Changing R06 from zero to 110 made it the first record in both reports, raised the total to 645 and removed the zero-count match. Restoring the source restored both full baseline orders. The native calculation engine and a browser view of the score-first report were checked. Blank keys, case-only ID differences, locale-specific collation and unresolved complete ties are outside this fixture; establish those policies for your own data.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Why is a lower score above a higher score?**

A: An earlier sort key can take priority. Department-first sorting groups departments before comparing scores within each group.

**Q: What does the number 2 in SORT mean?**

A: It is the second column within the selected input range, not necessarily worksheet column B.

**Q: Can I type notes beside a formula-sorted list?**

A: Keep notes keyed to the record ID. A manually entered adjacent note does not automatically move with a record when the formula recalculates.

## Downloads

- [Worked example](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/google-sheets-sort-multiple-columns/example.csv)
- [sort-input.csv](https://jhsoftlabs.com/samples/google-sheets-sort-multiple-columns/sort-input.csv)

```text
record_id,department,score,owner
R03,Sales,90,Ada
R01,Support,80,Bea
```

```text
Multi-column SORT practice checklist

E2:E8: =ISNUMBER(C2), filled down -> all TRUE.
```

# Google Sheets: Sum by Month and Category Without Mixing Years

**URL:** https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-sum-by-month-category
**Category:** dates
**Description:** Use SUMIFS to total a month and category in Google Sheets. Keep years separate and include late-night timestamps with an exclusive next-month boundary.

## Summary
Use SUMIFS with three criteria: the category matches, the timestamp is on or after the month's first day, and it is before the first day of the next month. Store each summary month as a real date, including its year. The exclusive upper boundary includes every time on the month's last day.

A monthly expense report needs a stable month-by-category grid, not just a list of discovered groups. A month-only condition can combine January from several years, and a date-only month-end condition can miss transactions recorded late on the final day.

## Worked example

```csv
booked_at,category,amount
2025-01-15 12:00:00,Travel,90
2026-01-01 00:00:00,Travel,40
2026-01-31 23:59:59,Travel,60
2026-02-01 00:00:00,Travel,80
2026-01-12 09:00:00,Office,25
2026-01-31 00:00:00,Travel,-10
2026-02-28 23:59:59,Office,35
2026-03-01 00:00:00,Office,45
```

**Expected:** January 2025 totals Travel 90 and Office 0. January 2026 totals Travel 90 and Office 25; February 2026 totals Travel 80 and Office 35; March 2026 totals Travel 0 and Office 45. The January 31 transaction at 23:59:59 belongs to January, and February 1 at 00:00:00 belongs to February.

### Prepare numeric timestamps and amounts

Import monthly-category-input.csv into a working sheet so its header starts at A1 and its eight records occupy A2:C9. A is booked_at, B is category, and C is amount. Keep the original download unchanged. The calculation requires numeric date-time values in A and numeric amounts in C. Check =ISNUMBER(A2) and =ISNUMBER(C2), then fill those checks down. A date-looking display does not prove that its underlying value is numeric.

For this fixed-width sample only, text timestamps can be converted in D2 with the formula below. Fill D2:E2 down only for rows whose A value is text in the exact YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss shape. Every E result must be TRUE before copying the corresponding D values and pasting values only back into the working copy of A. DATE and TIME can normalize invalid components, so the round-trip comparison matters. Do not apply this substring formula to an already numeric timestamp, UTC text ending in Z, offset timestamps or fractional seconds.

```text
D2: =DATE(VALUE(LEFT(A2,4)),VALUE(MID(A2,6,2)),VALUE(MID(A2,9,2)))+TIME(VALUE(MID(A2,12,2)),VALUE(MID(A2,15,2)),VALUE(RIGHT(A2,2)))
E2: =IFERROR(TEXT(D2,"yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss")=A2,FALSE)
```

### Check missing values before trusting a total

After converting timestamp text, use the row check below in F2 and fill it through F9. All eight sample records should show Ready. A text amount such as a leading-apostrophe 40, an absent timestamp, a blank category or a blank amount needs review. Formatting a cell as Currency or Date is not a data conversion. A numeric zero is valid, and the negative adjustment must stay signed.

Review is a stop-and-check flag, not permission to delete the transaction or turn missing amounts into zero. Resolve missing values from the source and agree whether a genuinely absent amount means zero or unknown. The nonempty-category check does not validate spelling: keep Travel and Office consistent, without extra spaces. This example uses plain category names; names containing * or ? need a separate literal-match check because SUMIFS criteria can be patterns.

```text
=IFERROR(IF(AND(ISNUMBER(A2),LEN(TRIM(B2))>0,ISNUMBER(C2)),"Ready","Review"),"Review")
```

### Build the month and category grid

Use G1:I5 for the summary. Put month_start in G1, Travel in H1, and Office in I1. In G2:G5 enter =DATE(2025,1,1), =DATE(2026,1,1), =DATE(2026,2,1), and =DATE(2026,3,1). Each boundary must be the first day of its month at midnight. A midmonth date or a time component would make this a rolling interval instead of a calendar-month total.

Format the month column as mmm yyyy if you want compact labels. Keep the underlying dates; text labels such as Jan omit the year and are not a dependable boundary value. The expected CSV is a reference for this summary grid, not another transaction file.

| Summary month | Inclusive start | Exclusive end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jan 2025 | 2025-01-01 00:00:00 | 2025-02-01 00:00:00 |
| Jan 2026 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-02-01 00:00:00 |
| Feb 2026 | 2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 2026-03-01 00:00:00 |
| Mar 2026 | 2026-03-01 00:00:00 | 2026-04-01 00:00:00 |

**Figure: The year is part of the month**

Synthetic comparison: grouping by month number alone joins two different January reporting periods.

Travel is 90 for January 2025 and 90 for January 2026; a month-only January grouping would incorrectly combine them as 180 for either year's report.

Separate periods:
Jan 2025 | Travel 90
Jan 2026 | Travel 90

Month-only mistake:
January | Travel 180
Two years combined

### Enter SUMIFS once and fill across and down

Enter the formula in H2, fill it across to I2, then fill H2:I2 down through row 5. The amount, category, and timestamp source ranges stay fixed and cover the same eight records. H$1 changes to I$1 when copied right while keeping row 1; $G2 changes to $G3 when copied down while keeping column G. H3 is January 2026 Travel, so it should return 90.

The formula uses commas between arguments. Depending on your locale, the formula editor may require semicolons. The month boundary remains a date calculation, so it does not depend on spelling January in a particular language.

```text
=SUMIFS($C$2:$C$9,$B$2:$B$9,H$1,$A$2:$A$9,">="&$G2,$A$2:$A$9,"<"&EDATE($G2,1))
```

| Month in G | Travel in H | Office in I |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jan 2025 | 90 | 0 |
| Jan 2026 | 90 | 25 |
| Feb 2026 | 80 | 35 |
| Mar 2026 | 0 | 45 |

### Include the whole last day

The January 2026 Travel amount is 40 + 60 - 10 = 90. The 60 posted at 23:59:59 on January 31 must be included. A test that ends at less than or equal to January 31's midnight can miss it, because the timestamp is later than that date's start. In this fixture, <=DATE(2026,1,31) gives only 30 for January 2026 Travel; the correct <DATE(2026,2,1) upper boundary gives 90.

Using less than February 1 avoids guessing the last possible second or fractional second in January. Exactly midnight on February 1 is excluded from January and included in February. The same rule works across month lengths and the December-to-January year boundary.

**Figure: One boundary, no overlap**

Synthetic timestamp boundary example. The comparison is before the next month, not before the last day ends at an assumed precision.

January includes the 40, 60, and minus 10 Travel records. The 80 at exactly February 1 midnight belongs only to February.

January includes:
Jan 1 00:00:00 | 40
Jan 31 23:59:59 | 60
Jan 31 00:00:00 | -10

February includes:
Feb 1 00:00:00 | 80
January Travel total: 90
February Travel total: 80

### Keep the reporting time zone consistent

These sample timestamps represent local wall-clock time in one agreed reporting zone. They contain no UTC marker or offset. If your source is UTC and the report uses another zone, convert the timestamps into the reporting zone before applying month boundaries. An event near midnight can belong to a different local date.

Check File > Settings for the spreadsheet's locale and time zone, but do not assume a settings change rewrites arbitrary timestamp text from another system. Keep the source convention with the data. Also keep refunds or adjustments signed: the negative Travel amount reduces the total instead of being dropped.

### Extend every range when new transactions arrive

The worked formula deliberately stops at row 9. In a practice copy, put =DATE(2026,1,15) in A10, Travel in B10, and numeric 5 in C10. H3 remains 90 until all three source ranges are expanded: $C$2:$C$10, $B$2:$B$10 and $A$2:$A$10 (both timestamp criteria use that last range). Also fill the row-readiness check to F10.

After updating the formula and filling the summary again, January 2026 Travel is 95 and the full summary is 370. Other cells retain their baseline values. Undo this optional extra row when comparing against the expected CSV, which contains only the original eight records. For a recurring report, choose an agreed larger range or maintained table reference and ensure every source column covers the same rows.

### Check a zero or an unexpectedly large result

For the fixture, a zero for January 2026 Travel is wrong; start by inspecting numeric types, exact category spelling, and the month-start cell. A large January figure may indicate that several years were combined. Different-sized or shifted criteria ranges can also associate dates with the wrong amount.

For the unmodified fixture, =SUM(H2:I5) and =SUM(C2:C9) should both return 365. January 2026 Travel is 90; February 2026 Travel is 80. Inspect the last-second and exact-midnight records separately. Reconciliation is a check, not proof: omissions and duplicates can cancel each other, and a real summary must cover all intended months and categories. If you need to discover all categories automatically rather than maintain this fixed grid, the separate QUERY GROUP BY guide explains that different output.

[Build a dynamic grouped summary with QUERY](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-query-group-by)

[Check wildcard patterns versus literal category codes](https://jhsoftlabs.com/guides/google-sheets-sumif-wildcards-literal-text)

### Verified practice results

This synthetic example was calculated in Google Sheets on October 11, 2026. All eight month/category results matched the expected grid, totaling 365. January 2026 Travel was 90 with the next-month boundary and only 30 with the incorrect last-day-midnight boundary; combining January by month number alone returned 180. The valid timestamp conversions and Ready checks also passed, and the grid was inspected in the browser.

Adding the optional five-unit transaction left the fixed-range total at 90; extending every source range changed it to 95 and the full summary to 370. Removing the practice addition restored the baseline. Separate native checks marked missing values, a text amount and a source error for review while accepting zero and a negative amount. February 30 normalized to March 2 and failed the text round-trip check. These observations cover this fixed-format fixture and controlled input changes, rather than arbitrary timestamp formats, every locale or time-zone conversion.

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I use MONTH(A2)=1 to sum January?**

A: Only if combining January across all included years is intentional. For a particular reporting month, use actual start and next-month dates so the year is included.

**Q: Why are some transactions from the last day missing?**

A: A date-only upper bound represents midnight at the start of that day. Use a strict less-than comparison with the first day of the next month to include the entire final day.

**Q: Why does the formula return zero after I format dates?**

A: Formatting does not necessarily convert text to numeric date-time values. Check ISNUMBER for the source dates and amounts, then verify category text and the summary month cell.

```text
Column Harbor synthetic monthly category practice

Input: monthly-category-input.csv in A1:C9.
Expected: monthly-category-expected.csv; comparison reference, not appended input.

Only for text timestamps with exact YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss shape:
D2: =DATE(VALUE(LEFT(A2,4)),VALUE(MID(A2,6,2)),VALUE(MID(A2,9,2)))+TIME(VALUE(MID(A2,12,2)),VALUE(MID(A2,15,2)),VALUE(RIGHT(A2,2)))
E2: =IFERROR(TEXT(D2,"yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss")=A2,FALSE)
All E results must be TRUE before pasting D values back into working A.

F2: =IFERROR(IF(AND(ISNUMBER(A2),LEN(TRIM(B2))>0,ISNUMBER(C2)),"Ready","Review"),"Review")
Fill F2:F9. Every baseline row must be Ready.

G1: month_start
H1: Travel
I1: Office
G2: =DATE(2025,1,1)
G3: =DATE(2026,1,1)
G4: =DATE(2026,2,1)
G5: =DATE(2026,3,1)
H2: =SUMIFS($C$2:$C$9,$B$2:$B$9,H$1,$A$2:$A$9,">="&$G2,$A$2:$A$9,"<"&EDATE($G2,1))
Fill H2:I2, then H2:I5.
Expected H2:I5: 90/0; 90/25; 80/35; 0/45.

Optional added row, separate from canonical expected CSV:
A10: =DATE(2026,1,15)

C10: 5
```
